n-the-argument-in-three-numbers.title: The argument in three numbers
n-the-argument-in-three-numbers.intro:
The parent gave you Section 4's verdict. This level gives you what sits underneath it.

Four things, in order. The arithmetic behind each cell of the table. The convolution rows that the summary skipped. The exact point where the argument stops resting on a bound and starts resting on an observation. And how much weight the interpretability claim can actually carry.

chapters.title: Where the numbers in the table come from
chapters.body:
The comparison is pinned to one job, so that every row is priced on identical work. The job is this: map a sequence $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ to another sequence $(z_1,\dots,z_n)$, where each $x_i$ and each $z_i$ is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$. That is what the paper calls a hidden layer in a typical encoder or decoder.

Every cell in [[table-1]] follows from counting the operations that job takes. Start with cost.

[[complexity-per-layer|Per-layer cost]] is the first column. A [[self-attention]] layer scores every query against every key. There are $n$ queries and $n$ keys, so there are $n^2$ scores. Each score is a dot product over $d$ dimensions, which is $d$ multiplications. That gives $n^2 \cdot d$, or $O(n^2 \cdot d)$. Using those scores to weight the values costs the same again, which does not change the order.

A [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent]] layer spends its budget differently. It takes $n$ steps, one per position, and each step is a $d \times d$ matrix multiply against the hidden state. That is $n \cdot d^2$, or $O(n \cdot d^2)$.

Look at what changed places. In the attention cost, $n$ is squared and $d$ is linear. In the recurrent cost, $d$ is squared and $n$ is linear. That swap is the whole reason the columns disagree later.

That is the cost. Now how much of it can run at once.

[[minimum-sequential-operations|Sequential operations]] counts the steps that must happen one after another. The attention layer is a fixed chain of matrix multiplies, and the length of that chain does not depend on $n$ at all — a sequence of ten positions and a sequence of a thousand go through the same number of stages. So $O(1)$.

The recurrent layer cannot do that. To compute step $t$ you first need the state that step $t-1$ produced, and to get that you need step $t-2$. The dependency runs all the way back. Adding GPUs does not shorten a chain.

That is the [[sequential-computation-bottleneck]] restated as a column: $O(n)$.

The third column is [[maximum-path-length|path length]], which asks how far a signal has to travel to get from one position to another. Inside one self-attention layer, any position reads any other position directly. One hop. In an RNN, a signal leaving position 1 and arriving at position $n$ has to pass through $n$ states in turn, each one rewriting it on the way.

Now what the columns do not count. They do not count constant factors, they do not count memory, and they do not count wall-clock time. There is no measured entry anywhere in the table — every figure is derived by counting operations, not by running anything.

The $O(1)$ path is also bought rather than free. It is paid for by [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost|averaging attention-weighted positions]]: a single attention operation blends many positions into one weighted sum, and detail specific to any one of them can be blurred out in the blending. That is a loss of resolution, and the paper says [[multi-head-attention]] is there to counteract it.

[[theme-why-self-attention]] walks the rows one at a time.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: The convolution rows, and one concession
chapters.body:
The recurrent comparison is the headline. The [[convolutional-sequence-models|convolutional]] one is where the paper does more work, and where it is less comfortable.

Start with the structure. A single convolutional layer has a kernel of width $k$, and when $k < n$ that kernel spans only $k$ positions at a time. Two positions further apart than $k$ never appear inside the same window. So one convolutional layer does not connect all pairs of positions at all.

To connect them you stack layers. With contiguous kernels you need $O(n/k)$ of them. With [[dilated-convolutions|dilated]] kernels, whose taps are spaced apart so each layer reaches wider, you need $O(\log_k n)$.

Either way, the longest path between two positions grows with $n$. That is the same complaint the background section makes about the prior convolutional models: [[convs2s|ConvS2S]], where the operations needed to relate two positions grow linearly in their distance, and [[bytenet|ByteNet]], where they grow logarithmically. The [[extended-neural-gpu|Extended Neural GPU]] sits alongside them in the same group.

It is worth being precise about which of those two numbers you are being shown. The convolutional row of [[table-1]] prints $O(\log_k n)$, which is the dilated figure. The running text gives $O(n/k)$, which is the contiguous one. Same row, two different assumptions. The favourable assumption is the one that made it into the table.

That is path length. Now cost, where convolutions come off worst.

A convolutional layer costs $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$. Set that next to the recurrent layer's $O(n \cdot d^2)$ and the difference is a factor of $k$ — the convolution pays for the whole kernel width on top of everything the recurrent layer already paid.

And then the paper argues against itself. [[separable-convolutions|Separable convolutions]] split the operation into a per-channel part and a mixing part, which cuts the cost to $O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$. The paper notes that even at $k = n$, the widest kernel there is, that figure equals the combined cost of a self-attention layer plus a [[position-wise-feed-forward-network|point-wise feed-forward layer]].

That combination is exactly what a Transformer layer is.

So on the cost column, the paper's own configuration ties with the strongest convolutional option. It does not win there. The separation the paper claims is on path length, and on [[long-range-dependencies|what that shorter path means for learning dependencies between distant positions]]. It is not on arithmetic.

[[etheme-case-against-recurrence]] collects the comparison as one argument.

chapters.title: The joint that has to hold: n against d
chapters.body:
The two cost columns cross at $n = d$.

Below that point, $n^2 d < n d^2$, and [[self-attention]] is the cheaper layer. Above it, the inequality flips and a recurrent layer is cheaper. The base model sets $d_{model} = 512$. So the claim the paper needs, for its own cost column to be the favourable one, is that its sentences are shorter than 512 tokens.

It does not measure this.

What it does instead is appeal to how sentences are represented in the models it competes with. Those models use subword vocabularies — [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] and [[byte-pair-encoding|byte-pair]] — and for the paper's own runs those vocabularies hold about 32000 and about 37000 tokens. A vocabulary that size keeps most words whole, splitting only the rare ones into pieces. So a [[machine-translation|WMT]] sentence lands in the tens of tokens, comfortably inside the margin.

The training setup points the same way. Batches were built at roughly 25000 source tokens each, with sentences grouped by approximate length. That is consistent with the same picture of typical sentence length.

But consistency is not a guarantee. This is a statement about a data regime, not a bound. Push $n$ to a thousand and the sign flips — and the growth is quadratic all the way there, so the cost is climbing long before the crossover arrives.

The escape hatch is the table's fourth row. [[restricted-self-attention|Restricting attention to a neighborhood of size $r$]] around each output position drops the per-layer cost to $O(r \cdot n \cdot d)$, which is linear in $n$. It keeps the $O(1)$ sequential operations, since nothing about the restriction introduces a dependency between steps. And it pushes [[maximum-path-length|path length]] to $O(n/r)$.

Note what that last figure does. It puts $n$ back into the path column — the one number the whole argument was built to remove.

The row also stays a proposal. No value of $r$ is chosen, no model using it is trained, and [[table-1]] carries the row as an entry rather than as a result. The paper says it plans to investigate the approach in future work.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: The claim made with pictures
chapters.body:
Section 4 ends with a fourth benefit, one that sits outside the three criteria the rest of the section is built on: [[attention-interpretability|self-attention could yield more interpretable models]].

Read the verbs. Heads *could* yield interpretability. Many of them *appear* to exhibit behavior related to syntactic and semantic structure. That is two hedges in two sentences, and the reason for them is that the support here is qualitative rather than measured.

The evidence is a set of appendix pictures showing encoder [[self-attention]] distributions.

[[fig-3]] shows several of the eight heads following a long-distance verb-phrase link, "making … more difficult", reaching across the words that sit between the two parts.

[[fig-4]] is the sharper case. For the single word "its", head 5 sends almost all of its weight to "Law", and head 6 sends almost all of its weight to "application". Two heads, two different resolutions of the same pronoun.

[[fig-5]] puts two heads from one layer side by side on one sentence, and shows that their patterns are plainly not the same.

What all three support is the [[multi-head-attention]] design: the idea that an [[attention-head]] specializes rather than replicating what its neighbors already do.

What they do not do is score anything. The sentences are chosen, not sampled. There is no count of how many heads turn out to be interpretable. There is no agreement measure against a parse. There is no comparison against what a recurrent model's attention looks like on the same input.

That is the shape of Section 4 as a whole. It contains no experiment. [[table-1]] is derived, and the interpretability claim is illustrated.

Whether the swap actually buys quality is left entirely to the results.

Applications of Attention in our Model

n-training-the-thing.title: Training the thing
n-training-the-thing.intro:
The parent listed the settings. This level takes them apart.

Start with the vocabulary counts, which nobody picks directly — they fall out of a procedure. Then the twelve hours: where they go, and how they turn into the cost axis of the comparison table. Then the learning-rate formula, and what it does at each end of the run.

Underneath all of it runs one distinction worth holding onto. Some of these pieces the paper tests. Most of them it merely reports.

chapters.title: The data, and what the token counts hide
chapters.body:
Start with the corpora, because they are the least interesting part of this. Both are standard benchmark sets, used the way everyone else uses them.

The vocabulary numbers attached to them are worth a second look. Those numbers are not chosen directly.

For [[wmt-2014-en-de|English-German]] the paper uses [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]]. A BPE vocabulary is not a word list that someone sat down and wrote. It is the output of a procedure: [[bpe-merge-algorithm|start from characters and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair]]. Every time that loop fires, one new symbol joins the inventory.

So [[bpe-vocabulary-size|the only knob is how many merges you run]]. The final symbol count is the starting character inventory plus the merge count, and nothing else enters into it.

Which means "about 37000 tokens" is a merge budget, not a word list. It is also the one number that decides how rare words get split.

That is the count. Now the sharing.

The vocabulary is shared between source and target. That is [[joint-bpe-shared-vocabulary|joint BPE]]: the merges are learned over both languages' text together, rather than once per language. The consequence is that the same string segments the same way on either side of the translation.

The sharing does a second job as well. It is what makes [[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing|the one-matrix embedding scheme]] possible at all. Encoder input, decoder input, and output projection can only be the same table if both languages index the same rows.

[[wmt-2014-en-fr|English-French]] switches schemes. It uses a 32000-token [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] vocabulary from [[wordpiece-model|Google's NMT system]]. No reason for the switch is given.

Both schemes carry the same [[vocabulary-vs-sequence-length-tradeoff|trade]], though. Split words more finely and the vocabulary shrinks, because fewer distinct pieces cover more text. Split more finely and every sentence gets longer, because each word now costs several tokens instead of one. The two move in opposite directions, and picking a merge count is picking a point on that curve.

That trade feeds straight back into Section 4's cost argument. Subword sentences stay short enough that $n < d$ — the sequence is shorter than the model is wide. And $n < d$ is exactly the condition self-attention's [[complexity-per-layer|$O(n^2 \cdot d)$ per-layer cost]] needs in order to come out ahead.

Now the batching. Batches are counted in tokens rather than in sentences: [[length-based-batching|about 25000 source tokens and about 25000 target tokens each]], with pairs of similar length grouped together.

Those are two separate decisions buying two separate things. Grouping by length keeps padding down, since a short sentence is never sitting in a batch sized for a long one. Counting in tokens keeps the per-step work roughly constant even as sentence lengths vary.

Spread across 8 GPUs, 25000 target tokens works out to on the order of 3000 target tokens per device per step.

chapters.title: Twelve hours, taken apart
chapters.body:
Twelve hours is the number half the paper's argument rests on. So multiply it out.

Start with the hardware. [[training-hardware-and-schedule|One machine, eight P100s]]. No cluster, no asynchronous workers — one box.

The base model runs 100,000 steps at about 0.4 seconds a step. That is roughly 40,000 seconds. Forty thousand seconds is a little over eleven hours, which the paper rounds to twelve.

The [[base-vs-big-transformer|big model]] runs 300,000 steps at about 1.0 seconds a step. That comes to 3.5 days. Three times as many steps, and two and a half times the cost of each step — the two factors multiply, so the big run is about 7.5 times the base run in GPU time.

That is what the clock says. Now what a step actually buys.

Each step processes 25,000 target tokens. Across 100,000 steps that is 2.5 billion target tokens seen during training.

The paper never reports epochs. But against a corpus of 4.5M sentence pairs, 2.5 billion tokens works out to something on the order of twenty passes — and how close to twenty depends on the average sentence length, which is not given.

That is the training budget. The cost axis in [[table-2]] is built from exactly these two numbers plus one assumption.

The recipe for that axis is [[training-flops-estimate|training time, times GPU count, times an assumed sustained throughput per GPU]]. The assumed throughput is 9.5 TFLOPS for a P100. Twelve hours on eight of them gives $3.3 \times 10^{18}$; 3.5 days gives $2.3 \times 10^{19}$.

Those are the figures printed in the table. Nothing on that axis was measured.

The step time is also where the architecture's claim cashes out. Follow one batch of 25,000 tokens through a single sub-layer. It goes through as one large matrix multiply — not as a chain of dependent updates — because [[minimum-sequential-operations|the number of operations that must run one after another]] does not grow with the sequence length. It is constant.

A [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent]] model of similar width cannot fill eight GPUs the same way. To get the hidden state at position 5 it needs position 4, and to get position 4 it needs position 3. Adding GPUs does not shorten a chain.

That is the [[sequential-computation-bottleneck]], showing up in wall clock rather than in asymptotics.

chapters.title: The one piece the paper invents
chapters.body:
Take the optimizer first, since it is borrowed, and then the schedule, which is not.

The optimizer is [[adam-optimizer|Adam]], run at [[transformer-adam-settings|$\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.98$, $\epsilon = 10^{-9}$]]. Two of those three are the usual values. $\beta_2$ is the odd one: 0.98, where the common default is 0.999.

What that changes is the memory of the running average of squared gradients. At 0.999 that average pools over a long stretch of past steps. At 0.98 the memory is shorter, so the per-parameter step size tracks a changing gradient scale faster.

The paper states the value. It gives no reason for it.

That was the borrowed piece. The [[learning-rate-warmup-schedule|schedule]] is where the behavior is. [[eq-lrate|Equation (3)]] makes the rate a minimum of two terms:

$$lrate = d_{model}^{-0.5} \cdot \min\left(step^{-0.5},\ step \cdot warmup^{-1.5}\right)$$

Take the two terms inside the minimum one at a time. The term $step \cdot warmup^{-1.5}$ grows linearly with the step number. The term $step^{-0.5}$ falls as the inverse square root of it. Early in training the linear term is the smaller of the two, so it wins the minimum and the rate ramps up. Later the decaying term is smaller and takes over.

The two are equal exactly at $step = warmup\_steps$. That equality is what joins the linear ramp to the inverse-square-root decay without a jump at the seam.

Now put the numbers in. With [[warmup-steps-4000|$warmup\_steps = 4000$]] and [[d-model|$d_{model} = 512$]], the peak rate is the value at that seam: $512^{-0.5} \cdot 4000^{-0.5} \approx 7 \times 10^{-4}$. And 4000 steps out of the base run's 100,000 is 4% of the run, so the peak arrives early and almost everything after it is decay.

By step 100,000 the rate is down to about $1.4 \times 10^{-4}$. Put another way: the step count has grown 25-fold since the peak, and the decay goes as the inverse square root, so the rate falls by a factor of 5. A fifth of the peak, across the whole run.

The $d_{model}^{-0.5}$ factor out front does something else. It ties the rate to the model's width, so a wider model automatically gets a smaller rate.

The big model is twice as wide, at $d_{model} = 1024$. That factor therefore shrinks by $\sqrt{2}$, and the peak lands near $5 \times 10^{-4}$ — with nobody retuning anything.

On evidence, be blunt. This schedule is one of the few pieces the paper introduces with no citation and no derivation. It is also not tested.

[[transformer-ablations|The ablations]] in [[table-3]] vary the head count, the key size, the width, the dropout rate, and the [[positional-encoding]]. The warmup length is not varied. Neither is the decay exponent, and neither is the width scaling.

The schedule is reported, used, and left alone.

chapters.title: Three regularizers, and where each one acts
chapters.body:
Placement is the part the summary skipped, so take each regularizer at the point in the network where it actually acts.

[[residual-dropout|Dropout is applied to each sub-layer's output before it is added back and normalized]]. The order there is the whole point. The dropped units never reach [[layer-normalization]], and the identity path through the [[residual-connection]] is left untouched.

Put another way: the sub-layer's contribution can be thinned, but the signal travelling along the shortcut cannot be cut.

Dropout hits one more place. It is applied to the sums of embeddings and [[positional-encoding|positional encodings]], in both stacks. So the position signal itself gets dropped out during training, right along with the token content it is added to.

That is where dropout acts. Now the rate.

It is $P_{drop} = 0.1$ for the base model. The big English-German model raises it to 0.3. The big English-French model goes back down to 0.1.

Same architecture, same size, different rate. The thing that changed between those two big runs is the data: 36M sentence pairs instead of 4.5M.

So the rate tracks data size, not model size. It is the one place where the recipe visibly adapts to the task.

[[size-and-dropout-ablation|Rows (C) and (D)]] of the ablation table are the support offered for the two claims underneath: bigger models are better, and dropout helps against overfitting. A separate [[attention-dropout|attention dropout]] rate exists as well, but it is mentioned only in the parsing experiments.

The second regularizer is [[label-smoothing]], at $\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1$. It is applied by citation — the value is set, and the mechanism is left to the cited paper.

[[label-smoothing-regularization|That mechanism]] replaces the one-hot target with something softer. The correct token gets $1 - \epsilon$ instead of 1, and the leftover $\epsilon$ is spread over the rest of the vocabulary.

[[smoothing-parameter-epsilon|$\epsilon$ and the prior distribution]] are its two knobs: how much mass to move, and where that mass goes. And [[lsr-as-two-cross-entropy-losses|the loss splits into two pieces]] — the ordinary cross entropy, plus a term pulling the prediction toward that prior.

[[overconfidence-and-bounded-logit-gradient|The stated motivation]] concerns what a one-hot target demands of the model. A one-hot target is only reached by driving the correct logit far above all the others.

The reported effect then splits in two directions. [[perplexity]] gets worse. [[bleu]] gets better.

That is not a contradiction. Perplexity grades how much confidence the model placed on the reference token, and smoothing deliberately holds that confidence back. BLEU grades the tokens decoding actually picks.

chapters.title: What you actually ship
chapters.body:
Training ends, and the weights you keep are not the weights from the last step.

[[checkpoint-averaging|The final model is the elementwise average of the last several checkpoints]]. Five of them for base models, twenty for big ones, written at ten-minute intervals.

Do the arithmetic on that window. Five checkpoints ten minutes apart span the last fifty minutes of a twelve-hour run. Twenty of them span the last two hundred minutes of an eighty-four-hour run.

Both are roughly the final 4% of training. That is the same fraction the warmup occupies at the other end.

So the averaging window is short. And it is scaled to the length of the run rather than fixed.

One consequence matters for reading everything else in the paper. Every number reported is an averaged model. No unaveraged checkpoint is reported anywhere, for any configuration.

Which leaves a question this paper cannot settle. There is no way, from what is printed here, to say how much of the headline quality comes from the architecture and how much comes from the averaging. The two arrive together.

The code is released as [[tensor2tensor]]. That release is the reproducibility claim, standing in place of a hyperparameter appendix.

Stand back from [[transformer-training-recipe|the whole recipe]] and one pattern holds. Of everything in this section, only the learning-rate schedule originates here.

Adam, dropout, [[label-smoothing]], [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]], word pieces, checkpoint averaging: each one is used at a stated setting, with a citation, and no re-derivation. Each [[etheme-borrowed-recipe|traces back to the papers that define them]].

And none of it is ablated. [[theme-training-the-thing|The training setup]] is reported, not tested. The one-knob-at-a-time experiments that come later touch the architecture, not this.

n-what-the-numbers-show.title: What the numbers show
n-what-the-numbers-show.intro:
The parent gave the headline figures. This level walks the path a number actually travels, from trained weights to a printed score.

Four questions, in order. What happens between a set of weights and a score. Which rows in the headline table the claim is beating, and by how much. What each ablation row does and does not license. And how much of the parsing result is generalization rather than tuning.

chapters.title: From weights to a score
chapters.body:
Start with the weights themselves. Nothing is decoded from the final weights of a training run.

The evaluated model is [[checkpoint-averaging|the elementwise average of the last checkpoints]] — five of them for base models, twenty for the big ones, written ten minutes apart. Average a set of saved snapshots parameter by parameter and you land on a point in weight space that no gradient step ever visited. So every figure in [[table-2]] belongs to a model that was never trained directly.

[[table-3]] is decoded without that averaging. That is one reason its numbers sit below Table 2's, and one reason the two tables cannot be read against each other.

Then the decoding itself. [[beam-search|Beam search]], with four hypotheses kept alive at each step.

Beam search scores a partial hypothesis by summing the log-probability of its tokens. Every token contributes a negative term. So a longer hypothesis accumulates more negative terms than a shorter one, and the raw sum quietly favours short outputs.

[[length-normalization-penalty|The cited length-normalization divisor]] is the correction: the summed score is divided by a function of hypothesis length. [[length-penalty|$\alpha = 0.6$]] is the strength knob on that function. At $\alpha = 0$ there is no normalization at all. At $\alpha = 1$ the score is divided by the full length. 0.6 sits between the two. The paper gives the value and not the formula.

The decoder the paper cites carries more machinery than the paper takes from it. [[coverage-penalty|A coverage penalty]] is available — an extra term in the beam score that rewards hypotheses whose attention has spread across the whole source sentence instead of concentrating on part of it. It goes unused here.

[[beam-search-pruning-and-termination|Pruning and early stopping]] are taken. So is a cap on output length: [[inference-length-limit|input length plus 50 tokens]].

That is the decoding procedure. Now where its settings came from.

Beam size, $\alpha$, and the length cap were picked by experimenting on the development set, newstest2013. That is the same set the ablations run on. It is not newstest2014, which is where the headline [[bleu|BLEU]] scores come from. None of the three is ablated.

And none of the three is a property of the architecture. The parsing run re-tunes the beam to 21 and $\alpha$ to 0.3. These are settings for [[wmt-2014-en-de|this task and this data]].

chapters.title: Reading the headline table row by row
chapters.body:
[[table-2]] is ten systems on two test sets, with a cost estimate printed beside each score. Start with the rows that carry the claim.

On English-to-German, the best prior single model is MoE at 26.03 — an LSTM with a [[conditional-computation|sparsely gated mixture-of-experts layer]], which routes each input to a few sub-networks instead of running all of them. The best prior row of any kind is the [[convs2s|ConvS2S]] [[model-ensembling|ensemble]] at 26.36. The [[base-vs-big-transformer|big Transformer]] gives 28.4.

So the "more than 2.0 BLEU" in the text is $28.4 - 26.36 = 2.04$. That subtraction is against an ensemble, not against a single model. It is the strictest comparison the table makes available.

The base model is the cheaper story. It scores 27.3, which clears every row above it, at an estimated $3.3\times10^{18}$ FLOPs.

For scale, GNMT + RL is listed on the same language pair at $2.3\times10^{19}$ — roughly the big Transformer's entire training cost — for 24.6 BLEU.

[[wmt-2014-en-fr|English-to-French]] is the weaker result, and the paper's wording tracks that. Base scores 38.1, below the baselines, and no claim is made for it.

Big scores 41.8 in the table and 41.0 in the text. The ConvS2S ensemble is at 41.29, which sits above 41.0. Hence the careful phrasing: better than all previously published *single* models.

One more thing, about the cost column. It is not measured.

[[training-flops-estimate|It is training time × GPU count × an assumed sustained throughput]] — 9.5 TFLOPS for a P100, 2.8 for a K80. Those are nominal capacities rather than observed utilization, and they are being applied to other groups' hardware and other groups' training runs. Read the column as an order of magnitude.

The [[bleu|BLEU]] column is cross-paper in the same way: different preprocessing pipelines, different tokenization, and only what each paper chose to publish.

chapters.title: The one place the design is tested
chapters.body:
[[transformer-ablations|Table 3]] is the only experiment in the paper that varies the architecture. Every row is read against the base row: 4.92 [[perplexity]], 25.8 BLEU, 65M parameters, on newstest2013. A blank cell means "same as base".

Rows (A) sweep the head count [[num-heads-h|$h$]]. As $h$ changes, [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = 512/h$]] changes with it, so the width of each head shrinks as the number of heads grows and the total attention compute stays roughly fixed. Only the split changes.

One head gives 24.9 — [[attention-heads-ablation|the 0.9 BLEU gap]] the paper quotes. Sixteen heads give 25.8, tied with eight. Thirty-two give 25.4.

Read together, those numbers show a plateau somewhere around 8–16 heads and a fall past it. They do not show an optimum at 8.

Rows (B) shrink only $d_k$ and leave $d_v$ at 64: 25.1 at $d_k=16$, 25.4 at $d_k=32$. Both below the base 25.8.

[[key-size-ablation|The paper's own reading]] is that determining compatibility is not easy, and that something richer than [[dot-product-attention|a dot product]] as the [[compatibility-function|compatibility function]] may help. That is a point against the paper's own design choice, and it is left unpursued.

Rows (C) and (D) are [[size-and-dropout-ablation|the expected ones]]. Two layers instead of six costs 2.1 BLEU. Removing [[residual-dropout|dropout]] costs 1.2. [[label-smoothing]] is varied in this block too.

Row (E) swaps [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding|sinusoids]] for [[learned-positional-embedding|learned position embeddings]]: 4.92 PPL, 25.7 BLEU. Near-identical to base — on one run each.

Two caveats the caption itself states. The perplexity figures are per word-piece under the paper's [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] vocabulary, so they are not comparable to per-word perplexities reported elsewhere. And every row is a development-set number, decoded without [[checkpoint-averaging]].

chapters.title: Parsing, and what it is meant to prove
chapters.body:
[[constituency-parsing|Parsing]] is picked because it stresses the architecture where translation does not.

The output has to obey hard structural constraints — brackets that close, labels that nest. The output also runs much longer than the input. And RNN sequence-to-sequence models had not topped the board in small-data settings.

It is a sequence problem only after [[parse-tree-linearization|the cited linearization]] flattens the tree into a string of bracket-and-label tokens. Put another way: the tree is not something the model is handed, it is something the output string has to spell out correctly.

The setup is deliberately thin. Four layers, [[d-model|$d_{model}$]] of 1024. A 16K vocabulary for the WSJ-only run, 32K for the semi-supervised one.

Four things were tuned, and only four: the [[residual-dropout]] rate, the [[attention-dropout|attention dropout]] rate, the learning rate, and the beam. They were tuned on Section 22 of [[wsj-parsing-protocol|the standard protocol]]. Everything else is left at the English-German base settings.

Decoding uses beam 21, $\alpha = 0.3$, and a cap of input length plus 300.

[[table-4]] puts the WSJ-only model at 91.3 F1 on Section 23, trained on [[penn-treebank-wsj|about 40K hand-parsed sentences]]. Set that against three rows.

It is above [[berkeley-parser|the BerkeleyParser]] at 90.4. It is 3.0 above the RNN sequence-to-sequence parser whose setup it borrows, at 88.3. And it is below [[recurrent-neural-network-grammar|the RNNG]] at 91.7 — the exception the paper names rather than passes over.

In [[semi-supervised-parsing|the semi-supervised setting]], with [[semi-supervised-parsing-corpora|roughly 17M machine-parsed sentences]] added on top of the 40K, it reaches 92.7. That is the top of that block.

Two higher numbers sit in the table: 93.0 multi-task and 93.3 generative. Neither is offered as a comparison.

What the experiment supports is narrow, and it is stated as such — the architecture transfers to a second task with almost no task-specific tuning. One task. One run. Still text.

n-what-this-establishes.title: What this establishes, and what it does not
n-what-this-establishes.intro:
The verdict is already in. The architecture claim holds. The evidence sitting under that claim is thin in specific, identifiable places.

This level does the accounting number by number. What the headline comparison actually controls for. How much weight each ablation row can carry. Where the cost axis comes from. And which of the paper's own mechanisms the paper itself labels as guesses.

chapters.title: What the comparison controls for
chapters.body:
Start with what was actually run. The headline configuration is specific, and the specifics matter for what can be concluded from it.

The big [[transformer|Transformer]] trains for 300,000 steps. Each step takes about 1.0 seconds on [[training-hardware-and-schedule|eight P100 GPUs in a single machine]]. Three hundred thousand seconds is a little over 83 hours, which is the 3.5 days the paper reports.

The [[base-vs-big-transformer|base model]] is the same machine and a shorter run: 100,000 steps, 12 hours. That shorter run already sits above every earlier row on English-German.

Those two rows share an author list, a codebase, a data pipeline and a machine. They are the only two rows in [[table-2]] produced by one group under one procedure.

Every other row in that table came from somewhere else. A different lab, with its own preprocessing, its own vocabulary, its own tuning budget, its own hardware, in a different year. Two of those rows are [[model-ensembling|ensembles]], and they report into the same [[bleu|BLEU]] column as the single models. What separates them is a horizontal rule and nothing else.

[[convs2s|ConvS2S]] and GNMT+RL were tuned by people who were optimizing their own architectures. Nobody re-tuned them against this one. That is the normal standard for reporting results on [[wmt-2014-en-de|WMT 2014]] — the test set is fixed, so the numbers are comparable in the sense a leaderboard needs them to be.

But a leaderboard is not a controlled experiment on architecture. A controlled experiment would hold the pipeline fixed and change one component. Nowhere in the paper is the Transformer's attention swapped for recurrence with everything else held constant.

So the supported statement is narrower than "attention beats recurrence." It is this: on newstest2014, with each system run under its own authors' best reported setup, this architecture posts the highest published number, and the cost its authors spent is below the costs the other groups reported.

The two language pairs do not carry that caveat equally. On [[wmt-2014-en-de|English-German]] the margin is over 2.0 BLEU. A gap that size is large enough that differences in preprocessing and tuning are an unlikely full explanation for it.

On [[wmt-2014-en-fr|English-French]] the margin is under a point. There the caveat bites much harder, because a sub-point gap is exactly the size that pipeline differences could account for.

chapters.title: One run per row
chapters.body:
The ablations are a different table with a different measurement protocol, so begin with the protocol.

Everything in [[table-3]] is measured on newstest2013, the English-German development set. None of it uses [[checkpoint-averaging]]. Both of those choices mean these figures do not line up with the test numbers in Table 2 — they are not the same quantity and should not be read across.

Within Table 3, the base row is the reference point: 25.8 BLEU and 4.92 [[perplexity|per-wordpiece perplexity]]. Every other row is a single training run of a single variant. One run. No repeats.

Rows (A) are the fairest comparison anywhere in the paper, because of how they are constructed. The head count [[num-heads-h|$h$]] varies, and the per-head dimensions move with it: [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h$]]. Since $d_{model}$ is 512, eight heads gives each head $512/8 = 64$ dimensions, and doubling the head count halves the width of each one. Total attention compute therefore stays roughly constant across the row, and the only thing that really changes is how the same budget is partitioned.

Here is what the partition buys. [[attention-heads-ablation|One head scores 24.9, eight heads score 25.8, thirty-two heads fall back to 25.4]].

Now size those differences. From one head to eight is $25.8 - 24.9 = 0.9$ BLEU. From eight heads to thirty-two is $25.8 - 25.4 = 0.4$ BLEU. That is the entire case for a middling head count: a 0.9-point gap and a 0.4-point gap, each measured between two single runs on a development set, with no repeat run and no confidence interval attached.

So take the shape and not the location. Too few heads is worse, and too many heads is worse. Where exactly the peak sits is not something two unreplicated runs can pin down.

Row (E) is the same problem at a smaller scale. [[learned-positional-embedding|Learned position embeddings]] give 25.7 against the [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding|sinusoids']] 25.8, at the same perplexity. That is a tenth of a point, well inside whatever run-to-run wobble an unreplicated experiment has.

"Nearly identical" is the paper's own phrase for this row, and it is the honest one. Nothing in the row separates the two schemes.

Two results in the table do survive the thinness, and they survive for the same reason: their effects are larger than any plausible run-to-run wobble. Removing [[dropout]] costs 1.2 BLEU ([[size-and-dropout-ablation]]).

The second is [[key-size-ablation|shrinking $d_k$ on its own, which hurts]]. That one is worth marking, because it is the single measurement in the paper that argues against the paper's own design. A smaller key dimension degrading quality hints that the [[compatibility-function|dot-product compatibility function]] may be too simple a way to score a query against a key.

chapters.title: The cost axis, and the number that moves
chapters.body:
[[training-flops-estimate|The cost column]] is not a measurement. It is arithmetic: training time, times GPU count, times an assumed sustained single-precision throughput per GPU.

Those assumed rates are fixed in footnote 5, one per device: 2.8, 3.7, 6.0 and 9.5 TFLOPS for the K80, K40, M40 and P100 respectively.

Run the multiplication for [[base-vs-big-transformer|the base model]]. Twelve hours is 43,200 seconds, there are eight P100s, and the assumed P100 rate is $9.5 \times 10^{12}$ floating-point operations per second. That gives $8 \times 43{,}200 \times 9.5 \times 10^{12} \approx 3.3 \times 10^{18}$. The same multiplication with 3.5 days in place of 12 hours gives roughly $2.3 \times 10^{19}$ for the big model.

Nothing here was profiled. The rate that enters the product is nominal capacity, not observed throughput, and it is applied at full value to every system in [[table-2]] — including models trained years earlier on entirely different clusters.

That assumption is doing real work. A model whose compute is mostly large batched matrix multiplications and a model whose compute is mostly small sequential operations will not sustain the same fraction of peak. If those fractions differ — and there is no reason to assume they do not — then the estimate is biased, and it is biased in a direction the paper has no way to report.

One statement underneath the estimate needs no assumption at all. That is the wall clock: [[training-hardware-and-schedule|12 hours and 3.5 days on eight GPUs]], set against baselines whose own papers report their training in GPU-days.

That is the cost axis. Now the one quality number that moves depending on where you look.

The abstract reports 41.8 [[bleu|BLEU]] on English-French. Section 6.1 reports 41.0 for the same model. The paper does not reconcile the two figures anywhere.

The gap decides exactly one comparison, so it is worth naming which. The best earlier [[wmt-2014-en-fr|English-French]] entry listed in the table is a [[convs2s|ConvS2S]] [[model-ensembling|ensemble]] at 41.29.

At 41.8, the big model clears that ensemble. At 41.0, it does not. Which is presumably why Section 6.1's own sentence claims only to beat previously published *single* models — the weaker of the two numbers supports the weaker of the two claims.

That English-French run also differs from the recipe in another way. It used dropout 0.1 rather than 0.3. That is a per-task adjustment, and no ablation in the paper covers it.

chapters.title: How much the parsing result buys
chapters.body:
The [[constituency-parsing|parsing]] run is the only evidence in the paper that any of this generalizes beyond translation. Because it carries that whole load on its own, it is worth being exact about what it beats.

[[table-4]] reports F1 on [[penn-treebank-wsj|WSJ Section 23]], and it does so in two training regimes. Take them one at a time.

The first regime uses the treebank alone: roughly 40K hand-parsed sentences and nothing else. A 4-layer Transformer reaches 91.3 F1 there. That is above [[berkeley-parser|the BerkeleyParser]] at 90.4.

It is also below [[recurrent-neural-network-grammar|Dyer et al.'s RNN Grammar]] at 91.7. The paper names that exception itself rather than leaving it to be noticed.

The second regime is [[semi-supervised-parsing|semi-supervised]], and there the model reaches 92.7 — the top number in the table.

Two things qualify that second figure.

The first is what the extra data is. The roughly 17M additional sentences are [[semi-supervised-parsing-corpora|not hand-annotated]]. They are existing parsers' output over news text. So the semi-supervised regime is partly measuring something other than parsing ability: it is measuring how well the model absorbs another parser's decisions.

The second qualification is about the baseline the paper leans on. That baseline is the [[recurrent-neural-network|RNN]] sequence-to-sequence parser whose [[wsj-parsing-protocol|protocol this experiment borrowed]] wholesale — same data splits, same [[parse-tree-linearization|linearization]] of trees into token sequences, same evaluation.

Against that one baseline the Transformer wins by 3.0 F1 with the small training set and by 0.6 F1 with the large one. Borrowing the protocol is what makes this a clean like-for-like comparison. It also means the comparison happens inside a setup that another group designed around a recurrent model.

The claim all of this supports is narrow, and it is real. Only three things were touched for the new task — dropout, learning rate and beam size — tuned on the Section 22 development set. Every other hyperparameter was carried over unchanged from the English-German base model.

Under those conditions the architecture transfers to a task with two properties translation does not have: the output is longer than the input, and the output must satisfy hard structural constraints to be a well-formed tree.

What it does not do is test another modality, another language, or anything longer than a single sentence.

chapters.title: The parts the paper marks as guesses
chapters.body:
One way to find the soft spots is to read the verbs. Do that, and a short list of mechanisms turns out to be unmeasured — flagged as such by the authors themselves.

On the [[sqrt-dk-scaling|$1/\sqrt{d_k}$ divisor]], the phrase is "we suspect": the suspicion is that large dot products push the softmax into a flat region. Suspected, not shown.

On [[eq-posenc|the sinusoid bank]], the phrase is "we hypothesized" — the hypothesis being that the encoding of a position shifted by a fixed offset would be a linear function of the original encoding ([[relative-position-linearity]]).

The same section supplies the reason for keeping [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding|sinusoids]] even after row (E) came out level, and that reason is hedged too. Sinusoids "may allow" the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths beyond those seen in training. Nobody tested that by feeding the model a longer sequence.

The material on what individual heads do carries "appear to exhibit" and "seems related." The supporting evidence is [[fig-3]], [[fig-4]] and [[fig-5]]: three hand-picked sentences, with no quantity attached to any of them. [[attention-interpretability]] is offered as a side benefit of the architecture, not as a finding.

[[restricted-self-attention|Restricted attention]] sits in a slightly different category. Its $O(n/r)$ [[maximum-path-length]] is written down in the table, and then the idea is left as future work.

That one matters more than its length in the paper suggests. It is the only answer the paper offers to the $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ per-layer cost of self-attention, and that cost is the one that stops being acceptable as soon as $n$ is no longer smaller than $d$.

And one constraint is not removed at all.

[[sequential-computation-bottleneck|The bottleneck the paper attacks]] is the recurrent one at training time. To compute the hidden state at position 5 you need position 4, and to get position 4 you need position 3, so the positions inside one training example cannot be computed at the same time. Adding GPUs does not shorten a chain.

Self-attention removes that chain during training. It does not remove it during generation. [[auto-regressive-generation|The decoder still emits one token at a time]], which is $n$ sequential steps for an output of length $n$, each one waiting on the token before it.

Put another way: the parallelism the paper wins is on the input side of a training step, not on the output side of a decode. The conclusion lists making generation less sequential as a goal, not as a result.

The offset to all of this is that the code ships as part of [[tensor2tensor]]. Every number above is therefore checkable by anyone with eight GPUs — including the numbers for which the paper itself reports no variance.

Applications of Attention in our Model

n-the-shape-of-the-model--add-then-norma.title: Add, Then Normalize
n-the-shape-of-the-model--add-then-norma.intro:
The parent gave the order of operations. This level does three things with it.

It counts how many times that order actually runs. It writes out the normalization formula, which the paper leaves to its citation. And it separates what the paper measured about this wrapper from what it only inherited from the work it cites.

chapters.title: The wrapper, written out
chapters.body:
Start with what the compact notation hides, which is how much work $\mathrm{Sublayer}$ is doing. It is not the raw attention function.

For an attention [[sub-layer]], $\mathrm{Sublayer}$ is the whole [[eq-multihead|multi-head block]]. That includes the output projection $W^O$ at the end of it. For the other kind, it is all of [[eq-ffn|Equation (2)]] — a linear map, a ReLU, then a second linear map.

Everything up to and including that final projection lives on the branch. The addition sees only one thing: the branch's last output.

The wrapper is defined once and then applied without variation, so counting the sites is arithmetic.

The [[encoder-stack]] has [[n-layers|six layers]], and each of those layers holds two sub-layers. The [[decoder-stack]] also has six layers, but each of those holds three, because [[encoder-decoder-attention|encoder-decoder attention]] is inserted between [[masked-decoder-self-attention|masked self-attention]] and the feed-forward block.

Six times two is twelve. Six times three is eighteen. That is thirty wrapped sub-layers in the base model — thirty additions, thirty normalizations.

[[fig-1]] draws the wrapper as a single "Add & Norm" box, which is why the count is easy to miss.

It is worth being precise about what the untouched path buys, because the guarantee turns out to be narrower than the phrase suggests.

Within one wrapper, $x$ reaches the sum having passed through nothing. No scaling, no dropout — it arrives as it was.

But [[layer-normalization|the norm]] sits on the trunk rather than on the branch. So the clean addition path is exactly one sub-layer long. The input to sub-layer $k+1$ is the normalized output of sub-layer $k$, not a raw sum.

Put another way: between the embedding and the logits, the trunk crosses thirty normalizations. Nothing travels that whole distance untouched.

What each [[residual-connection|residual]] guarantees is local. This sub-layer starts from the identity, and it only has to learn a difference.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: The dropout, and the only evidence for it
chapters.body:
Section 5.4 is where the placement is actually stated. It names two applications of the same regularizer, not one.

[[residual-dropout|Residual dropout]] hits every sub-layer output before the addition. That is the first application. The second sits at the bottom of both stacks: the same dropout hits the sums of the [[token-embeddings|token embeddings]] and the [[positional-encoding|positional encodings]].

So the very first thing on the trunk is already a dropped-out vector. The identity path starts from a noisy embedding sum, not a clean one.

That is the placement. Now the rate, which is a single number.

The base model uses $P_{drop} = 0.1$ everywhere — every site, the same value. The [[base-vs-big-transformer|big model]] raises it to $0.3$ for English-to-German. Then, for English-to-French, it drops back to $0.1$; the paper's stated reason is the much larger dataset.

One knob, tuned per run, not per site.

The evidence for any of this is thin, and it is indirect.

[[table-3]] rows (D) vary the dropout rate on the base model. The paper's own reading of rows (C) and (D) is a single sentence: bigger models are better, and [[size-and-dropout-ablation|dropout is very helpful in avoiding over-fitting]].

That tests the rate. It does not test where the dropout goes.

Nothing in [[transformer-ablations|the ablations]] tests the placement. There is no run comparing dropping before the addition against dropping after it, and none comparing dropping the branch against dropping the sum.

The one hint that these are separable knobs comes from elsewhere. The [[constituency-parsing|parsing]] experiments say that residual and [[attention-dropout|attention dropout]] were tuned separately. The values are not reported.

chapters.title: The formula the paper does not print
chapters.body:
Written out for one position. Let $H = d_{model}$ be the number of activations arriving at the normalization site, and call them $a_1 \dots a_H$:

$$\mu = \frac{1}{H}\sum_{i=1}^{H} a_i, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{H}\sum_{i=1}^{H}(a_i - \mu)^2}, \qquad h_i = g_i\,\frac{a_i - \mu}{\sigma} + b_i$$

Take the three terms in order. $\mu$ is the mean of those $H$ numbers. $\sigma$ is their standard deviation. Each output $h_i$ is the matching input, centred by $\mu$, divided by $\sigma$, then scaled by $g_i$ and shifted by $b_i$.

Here $H = 512$. So [[layer-normalization-statistics|the mean and standard deviation]] are each an average over that one token's [[d-model|512 numbers]] — one token's numbers, not the batch's.

The vector being normalized is $x + \mathrm{Dropout}(\mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$. The addition has already happened. Normalization only ever sees the merged vector.

One omission is worth marking. Neither this paper nor the cited one writes the $\epsilon$ that a real implementation puts under the square root.

The [[gain-and-bias-parameters|gain $g$ and bias $b$]] are the only learned parameters the wrapper adds. They are cheap, and the count shows how cheap.

Each is a vector of length 512, so a site adds $2 \times 512 = 1024$ numbers. Across all thirty sites that is about 31k parameters, against roughly 65M for the base model.

They are indexed by unit, not by position. [[per-timestep-normalization|One set of 1024 numbers is shared by every token in the sequence]]. That sharing is what lets a normalization site accept a sequence of any length.

Without $g$ and $b$, the operation would be a pure standardization — every output forced to the same mean and variance. Each [[sub-layer]] would then be unable to express a scale of its own.

Note what does not happen.

The statistics are recomputed from scratch at each of the thirty sites, for each position, on every forward pass. There is no running average. Nothing is carried from training into inference — [[layer-normalization]] has no state.

chapters.title: Why this normalizer and not the other
chapters.body:
That stateless property from the last chapter is the whole argument for this normalizer over the obvious alternative.

[[layer-norm-vs-batch-norm|Batch normalization slices the activation tensor the other way]]. It fixes one neuron and takes its statistics across the mini-batch.

In a sequence model, that slice has to be taken per time step. And step $t$'s statistics come only from those sentences in the batch that are long enough to reach $t$. A sentence of twenty tokens contributes nothing at position forty.

Which sentences share a batch is therefore not an incidental detail here. This paper builds batches by [[length-based-batching|grouping sentence pairs of similar length]], to about 25000 source and 25000 target tokens each.

So batch membership is a function of the packing. The late positions of a long sentence would be normalized by whatever few samples remain.

There is a second cost. Batch norm would also need stored running statistics for inference. And inference here is [[beam-search|beam search]], which presents whatever number of hypotheses it happens to be holding.

[[per-timestep-normalization|Normalizing across the 512 units of one position instead]] removes every one of those dependencies.

The arithmetic for a token is identical in a full training batch, in a batch of one, and mid-decode.

The cited work adds a second claim, which this paper inherits without restating.

[[normalization-invariance-properties|Scaling a layer's weight matrix leaves its normalized output unchanged]]. The gradient with respect to those weights shrinks in proportion to that same scaling. So the effective step size adapts to the weight scale on its own.

That is the mechanism behind the faster-training claim.

All of this is imported. Nothing in this paper measures it. There is no run reported with the normalizer removed, moved, or swapped.

n-one-operation--what-the-heads-buy.title: What the Split Is Shown to Buy
n-one-operation--what-the-heads-buy.intro:
The parent named the evidence. This level opens it.

Four things, in order. First, the exact rows of the sweep, and what was held fixed while the head count moved. Second, a confound that the protocol builds in rather than controls for. Third, a row in the same table that turns on the paper's own scoring rule. Fourth, the three appendix pictures, and what each one can carry.

chapters.title: The five rows, and what was held fixed
chapters.body:
Start with the structure. Group (A) of [[table-3]] is five rows: four separately trained models, plus the base row as the reference point.

The base row is the configuration the rest of the paper uses. It has [[num-heads-h|$h = 8$]] heads, each one with [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = 64$]]. It scores 4.92 [[perplexity|PPL]] and 25.8 [[bleu|BLEU]], at 65M parameters.

The four variants move the head count down and up around that base.

One head, with $d_k = d_v = 512$, gives 5.29 and 24.9. Four heads at 128 gives 5.00 and 25.5. Sixteen heads at 32 gives 4.91 and 25.8. Thirty-two heads at 16 gives 5.01 and 25.4.

The pairing inside each of those settings is not incidental. Head width is tied to head count by the rule $d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h$. Check it against the rows: one head times 512, four times 128, eight times 64, sixteen times 32, thirty-two times 16. Every one of those products is 512. So $h \cdot d_k = 512$ in every row of the group.

That identity is what holds the computation constant. The concatenation of all the heads is always [[d-model|512]] wide, whatever $h$ happens to be. [[attention-projection-matrices|$W^O$]], the matrix that mixes that concatenation back into the model, is therefore always $512 \times 512$. And the per-head query, key, and value projections always sum to the same total width. Parameter count stays at 65M across the whole group.

That is the sense in which one head and thirty-two heads cost the same. Not an estimate. An identity built into how the rows were chosen.

Now the measurement itself. The numbers come from newstest2013, the English-to-German development set. Decoding used [[beam-search]], and it did not use [[checkpoint-averaging]]. Two consequences follow. These are not the numbers from the headline table, and they are not test-set numbers at all.

The perplexities carry a caveat of their own. They are per word-piece, under the paper's [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] vocabulary, and the caption says they should not be compared to per-word perplexities reported elsewhere.

Each row is one run.

chapters.title: Head count and head width move together
chapters.body:
The identity that keeps the computation constant is also what limits the reading. Because [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h$]], the head count and the head width cannot move independently. Change one and the other changes with it.

So the row labels mislead if they are read as head counts alone. The $h = 1$ row is not "one head" — it is one head 512 dimensions wide. The $h = 32$ row is thirty-two heads, each of them only 16 dimensions wide.

Both ends of the curve therefore have two candidate explanations, and [[attention-heads-ablation|the sweep]] cannot tell them apart. Take the falloff at 32 heads. It is as consistent with 16-dimensional keys being too narrow to score a match as it is with there simply being too many heads.

The paper's own group (B) is the reason to take that alternative seriously: [[key-size-ablation|shrinking $d_k$ alone hurts]], and at $d_k = 16$ most of all. Put another way, the paper shows elsewhere in the same table that narrow keys damage quality by themselves — and narrow keys are exactly what the $h = 32$ row also has.

Now the top of the curve, which is flat in a way worth naming. Sixteen heads posts the group's best perplexity, 4.91 against the base row's 4.92, and ties the base row on BLEU at 25.8.

The base model ships [[num-heads-h|eight]] heads anyway, and [[table-3]] gives no reason for the choice.

With one run per setting, and no seeds and no intervals reported, a 0.01 perplexity difference is not a signal anyone should act on. And the 0.9 BLEU quoted for this sweep is the distance from the worst row in the group to the best. It is not a gradient anywhere near $h = 8$.

That leaves the claim the split was introduced to answer, which none of this touches. [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost|Averaging blurring position-specific information]] is a statement about representations — about what collapsing many positions into one weighted sum does to information tied to particular positions. Group (A) reports end-task BLEU.

No number anywhere measures resolution retained. [[multi-head-attention|The design]] is defended by a proxy.

chapters.title: Row (B) turns on the scoring rule
chapters.body:
Group (B) breaks the tie that the previous group enforced. Head count stays at eight. $d_v$ stays at 64. Only the key dimension shrinks.

At $d_k = 32$: 5.01 PPL, 25.4 BLEU, 60M parameters. At $d_k = 16$: 5.16 PPL, 25.1 BLEU, 58M parameters. Both rows are worse than base on both metrics, and the effect is monotone — the smaller the key, the worse the model.

But note what this group gives up in exchange. It is not compute-neutral the way group (A) was. The query and key projections genuinely shrink, which is why the parameter count falls too, from 65M to 60M to 58M. Parameters fall alongside quality here, so model size is a live alternative explanation for the drop.

Section 6.2 draws a conclusion anyway, in one sentence: determining compatibility is not easy, and a more sophisticated [[compatibility-function]] than a dot product may be beneficial.

That is the authors casting doubt on their own scoring rule, inside the same table that defends their head count.

It also lands next to an admission the paper had already made, back in Section 3.2.1. There, the paper grants that [[additive-attention]] outperforms unscaled [[dot-product-attention|dot products]] at large $d_k$ — which is the reason [[sqrt-dk-scaling|the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ divisor]] is in the formula at all. So the large-$d_k$ end already had a known problem. Row (B) probes the small-$d_k$ end, and finds trouble there too.

What [[key-size-ablation|the row]] does not do is test the alternative it points at. There is no additive-attention row in the table, at any budget.

So the step from "small keys hurt" to "the dot product may be too simple" is an inference, not a measurement, and the paper marks it as a suggestion. [[scaled-dot-product-attention|The function]] survives the section unchanged.

chapters.title: Figure 3: eight heads, one dependency
chapters.body:
[[fig-3]] draws a single query position. The layer is [[encoder-self-attention]] at layer 5 of [[n-layers|six]]. The sentence ends "...passed new laws since 2009 making the registration or voting process more difficult."

Only the attention leaving one word, "making", is drawn. Each [[attention-head|head]] gets its own colour, and the opacity of a line carries the [[softmax]] weight that head put on that target.

Most of the visible mass lands on two words. Four heads — blue, orange, green, gray — concentrate on "more". Four — blue, green, red, brown — concentrate on "difficult". Those two words sit six and seven tokens after "making", with "the registration or voting process" in between. Two heads go elsewhere: a purple head attends back to "making" itself, and a pink head to "2009" and "laws".

Read as evidence for the eight-way split, this is the weakest of the three pictures, and for a specific reason. On the one word it draws, the heads mostly agree. Four heads doing the same job is redundancy, not division of labour.

What the picture does show cleanly is something else. A [[long-range-dependencies|long-distance dependency]] is crossed in a single hop, rather than in six sequential steps along the sentence. That is [[maximum-path-length|the path-length argument]] made visible.

The frame is narrow too. One query position, one sentence, one layer, one model.

The caption says "many of the attention heads" attend to the distant dependency. A reader cannot check that count against the figure, because only the lines leaving "making" are drawn. [[attention-interpretability|The observation is offered as an example]], not as a rate.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: Figures 4 and 5: two heads pulled apart
chapters.body:
The remaining two pictures share a sentence and a layer. The sentence is "The Law will never be perfect, but its application should be just — this is what we are missing, in my opinion". The layer is [[encoder-self-attention|encoder self-attention]], layer 5 of 6 again.

[[fig-4]] has two panels. The top panel shows all of head 5's attention across the sentence, mostly faint lines.

The bottom panel narrows to one word. It keeps only the lines leaving "its", and it draws them for two heads at once. Head 5 sends nearly all of that word's weight to "Law". Head 6 sends nearly all of it to "application".

The caption calls the attentions "very sharp" for this word, and calls the behaviour "apparently involved in anaphora resolution".

This is the clearest instance of the diversity claim anywhere in the paper. Two [[attention-head|heads]] at the same depth give one token two different answers, on a job nobody supervised.

It is also one pronoun, in one sentence.

[[fig-5]] is two full attention maps, from the same layer, for two different heads. The green head spreads a haze across nearly every pair of positions, with heavy fans converging on Law, application, missing and opinion. The red head is sparse: short, near-vertical links picking out one or two nearby tokens.

Also visible in both panels is a dark self-link on `<pad>`. Not every strong line in these maps is linguistic, and nothing in the figure sorts the linguistic ones from the rest.

The captions grade themselves unevenly, and Section 4 keeps the same split. That the heads "clearly learned to perform different tasks" is stated flat. That the behaviour is related to syntax and semantics only "seems" so.

[[attention-interpretability|Interpretability]] is named a side benefit. No layer other than the fifth is shown, and nothing is scored.

n-three-wirings-of-the-same-block--all-p.title: The encoder: an all-pairs mixer, six times over
n-three-wirings-of-the-same-block--all-p.intro:
One level up gave the shape of the layer. This one goes down to the tensors, and to the bill.

Four things, in order. What an encoder layer actually multiplies. What kind of claim Table 1's path-length row is making. How a representation at layer 5 differs from the same representation at layer 1. And how much the three appendix pictures establish.

chapters.title: One layer, in tensors
chapters.body:
Start with one layer, and inside it one head.

The input is whatever the previous layer produced: $n$ rows, each of width [[d-model|512]]. Three learned matrices $W^Q, W^K, W^V \in \mathbb{R}^{512 \times 64}$ act on those rows. Each one projects every row from 512 down to [[dk-dv-dimensions|64]].

The three results are the [[queries-keys-values|queries, the keys and the values]]. All three are read off the same $n$ rows. That is the whole content of the word [[encoder-self-attention|self-attention]] here — the thing doing the querying and the thing being queried are the same tensor.

Then the scoring. $QK^{T}$ multiplies every query against every key, which produces the $n \times n$ block: one number for each ordered pair of positions. Divide that block by $\sqrt{d_k}$, which with $d_k = 64$ is 8 ([[sqrt-dk-scaling]]). [[softmax]] each row so it becomes a set of weights. Multiply by $V$. What comes back out is $n \times 64$ — one blended value vector per position.

That is one head. [[num-heads-h|Eight]] of them run at once, each on its own three projections. Concatenate the eight $n \times 64$ outputs and the width is $n \times 512$ again, which then passes through one more matrix $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{512 \times 512}$ ([[eq-multihead]]).

The head width is not a free parameter. It is fixed by $d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h$: $d_{model}$ is 512, there are 8 heads, so each head gets $512/8 = 64$ dimensions. The point of setting it that way is cost — eight narrow heads together come to about what one full-width head would.

One more structural fact about the encoder. There is no mask, no truncation, no sub-sampling anywhere in it. Every row of every score matrix runs across the whole source.

Concretely, at the size the paper draws. The sentence in [[fig-3]] is padded out to 33 positions. 33 queries against 33 keys is 1089 scores per head. Eight heads makes 8712 scores per layer. Across [[n-layers|six]] layers that comes to roughly 52,000 query-key products — for one short sentence, in one direction, on one training step. [[fig-2]] is the same path drawn as a block diagram rather than as shapes.

Notice what that arithmetic is actually dominated by at that size. The $O(n^{2} \cdot d)$ figure the paper quotes for a self-attention layer counts two things: the scoring, and the blending of values that follows it.

It does not count the projections. Those — the ones producing $Q$, $K$ and $V$, plus the output projection — are per-position matrix multiplies of shape $O(n \cdot d^{2})$. That is the same shape a recurrent layer's computation has. And at $n = 33$ with $d = 512$, they are the larger term.

The table does not break them out.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: What the constant path buys, and what it costs
chapters.body:
[[table-1]]'s path-length row is why this wiring is in the paper at all. So read carefully for what kind of claim it is.

The row gives [[maximum-path-length|maximum path length]] $O(1)$ for a self-attention layer, against $O(n)$ for a [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent]] one. The neighbouring row gives [[minimum-sequential-operations|sequential operations]], again $O(1)$ against $O(n)$.

Both of those are hop counts in a computation graph. They are things you can read off the wiring. They are not measurements of anything a trained model did.

The step from short paths to the interesting conclusion is a separate step. Short paths are supposed to make [[long-range-dependencies]] easier to learn, and the paper asserts that step with a citation rather than testing it. Nothing in the paper swaps a self-attention encoder layer for a recurrent one and reports the difference. [[layer-comparison-desiderata|The three criteria]] are an argument, not an experiment.

The bill is in the other column. [[complexity-per-layer]] for self-attention is $O(n^{2} \cdot d)$, against a recurrent layer's $O(n \cdot d^{2})$.

Set those two side by side and the crossover falls out: self-attention is the cheaper of the two exactly when $n < d$. With $d = 512$, and with sentences cut into [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] or [[byte-pair-encoding|byte-pair]] units, the paper says this is most often the case.

That is a claim scoped to sentence-length inputs. Past a few hundred tokens the inequality turns over.

Section 4 names its own escape hatch, and then declines to use it. [[restricted-self-attention]] would let each position attend only to a neighborhood of size $r$ rather than to the whole sequence. That cuts the quadratic term. It also pushes path length back up to $O(n/r)$ — reaching across the sentence now takes several hops instead of one.

The paper reports no model built this way. It says it plans to investigate it in future work.

There is also a cost that no column in the table shows, and the background section admits it directly. Collapsing many positions into one weighted average reduces effective resolution ([[attention-averaging-resolution-cost]]). An average is lossy about which position contributed what.

[[multi-head-attention|Running eight heads]] is the stated counter to that. Which puts the head count in a particular light. It is a repair for a known weakness of the mechanism rather than a free extra.

chapters.title: Six rounds, and what the stack carries forward
chapters.body:
Six identical rounds could easily amount to mere repetition. What keeps them from being that is the wrapping.

Every [[sub-layer]] outputs $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$. That is a [[residual-connection]] first — the input $x$ added back to whatever the sub-layer computed — and then [[layer-normalization]] over the sum.

The consequence is that an attention sub-layer never replaces position 7's vector. It adds an increment to it.

Count that up the stack. At the top of layer 3, that vector is the embedding plus six sub-layer increments, normalized six times.

Now the two kinds of sub-layer, because they do different jobs. The attention sub-layers are the only place anything crosses between positions.

The other one is [[position-wise-feed-forward-network|the feed-forward network]], [[eq-ffn|$\max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2$]]: 512 up to $d_{ff} = 2048$, ReLU, back down to 512. It is applied to each position separately and identically, and it carries its own weights in each layer. The paper's alternative description of it is two convolutions of kernel size 1.

So the [[encoder-stack]] alternates. Mix across positions, then transform each position on its own. Six times ([[fig-1]]).

That alternation is what makes attending over the layer below different in kind at depth. In layer 1, the keys are projections of embeddings plus positional signal — close to the words themselves.

In layer 5, the keys are projections of vectors that have already been mixed across the whole sentence four times and pushed through four ReLU expansions. The dot product is scoring those, not words. Put another way: by layer 5 a query-key match is a comparison between two accumulated summaries.

One thing enters the stack exactly once. [[positional-encoding|Position]] is added at the bottom, to the embeddings, and never re-injected higher up.

So whatever order information reaches layer 5 has survived six rounds of weighted averaging on the residual path. The paper does not check that it does.

Nor does it say what any individual layer contributes. The layers are identical in shape and described as identical, and the only one it ever opens is the fifth.

chapters.title: The only layer the paper opens
chapters.body:
All three appendix pictures come from the same place. Layer 5 of [[n-layers|six]]. [[encoder-self-attention|Encoder self-attention]]. A trained translation model.

They also share a drawing convention. The sentence appears twice, lines run from a querying copy to an attended copy, and line opacity stands in for weight.

[[fig-3]] draws one query row out of 33 — the verb "making" — with the lines colored by [[attention-head|head]]. Blue, orange, green and gray pile onto "more". Blue, green, red and brown pile onto "difficult", with two heads appearing in both groups.

Those two words sit six and seven tokens later, with "the registration or voting process" in between. Separately, a purple head attends to "making" itself, and a pink one to "2009" and "laws". The other 32 query rows are not shown.

[[fig-4]] holds the sentence fixed and varies the head instead. Its top panel is head 5's full map, mostly faint lines. Its bottom panel keeps only what leaves the word "its": head 5 sends nearly all of it to "Law", head 6 nearly all to "application". The caption's operative word is "apparently".

[[fig-5]] is one more sentence, two heads, whole maps. One head spreads a haze across nearly every pair, with heavy fans converging on a few words. The other is sparse and short-range.

Its caption splits in two, and the two halves are held with different force. That the heads "clearly learned to perform different tasks" is stated flat. The tie to sentence structure only "seems" to hold.

So, added up: two sentences, one layer, chosen heads. No axes, no printed numbers, no counts over a corpus, opacity as the only quantitative channel. Section 4 files [[attention-interpretability|interpretability]] as a side benefit and hedges to heads that "appear to exhibit" such behavior.

The measured claim about heads sits elsewhere, and it says less. [[table-3]] varies $h$ with computation held constant. Single-head attention comes in [[attention-heads-ablation|0.9 BLEU below the best setting]], and too many heads is worse again.

What that establishes is that several heads help. What any one of them does is not in that number, and [[multi-head-attention]] is not otherwise probed.
