n-per-position-parts--one-matrix-three-j.title: The sentence that imports another paper
n-per-position-parts--one-matrix-three-j.intro:
Section 3.4 of the Transformer paper is two sentences and a citation. The two sentences state a design choice. The citation is where the reasoning for that choice lives, and the paper does not repeat any of it.

This level goes and reads the citation. Five things come back. What the two same-shaped matrices are. What the gradient argument for tying actually says. What the translation variant was measured to buy. What vocabulary that variant demands. And last, the one clause of Section 3.4 that arrives with no argument at all.

chapters.title: Two matrices, one shape
chapters.body:
The citation points at a paper about language models, not about translation. Its setup is worth restating in its own notation rather than the Transformer's. That is where the two roles get named, and the naming is the part that carries over.

Start with the shapes.

Take a vocabulary of size $C$ and a hidden width $H$. [[input-and-output-embeddings|Two matrices]] in such a model come out the same size, $C \times H$: one row per vocabulary item, one column per hidden dimension.

The first is the input embedding $U$. It is an ordinary [[token-embeddings|lookup table]]. A one-hot token $c$ becomes $U^{\top}c$, which just selects a single row, so row $U_k$ is word $k$'s vector.

The second sits at the other end of the model. The network computes a hidden state $h$, and a matrix $V$ turns that state into logits, $Vh$. Each entry of $Vh$ is an inner product of $h$ with one row of $V$. So row $V_k$ is the vector whose inner product with $h$ gives word $k$'s score, before the [[softmax]] turns those scores into probabilities.

Two matrices, one shape, one at each end. Standard practice was to call $U$ the word embedding and throw $V$ away.

The cited paper's claim is that $V$ is a word embedding too. It is arrived at for a different reason than $U$ is. $U$ wants near rows for synonyms, so that the network reacts the same way to either word when it comes in. $V$ wants near rows for interchangeable words, so that their scores come out alike when the model is deciding what comes next.

The paper checks this rather than asserting it. It scores $V$ on word-similarity benchmarks, the same way one would score any embedding. In skip-gram models $V$ lands roughly level with $U$. In recurrent [[language-modeling|language models]] it lands ahead of $U$.

That measurement is the premise everything else rests on. If the output matrix were junk, sharing it with the input would be a pure loss.

One precondition rides along with the whole idea. The constraint only typechecks when the embedding width and the width of whatever enters the pre-softmax projection are the same number. If those differ, an extra projection has to be spliced in between, and the scheme stops being free.

In the Transformer that never comes up. Everything is [[d-model|512 wide]], including whatever the [[decoder-stack|decoder]] hands to the output projection. The constraint costs nothing, so the paper never has to mention it.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: What the sum of two gradients contains
chapters.body:
[[weight-tying|Tying]] is the constraint $U = V = S$. One matrix occupies both slots.

There is no extra loss term pulling the two toward each other, and no stop-gradient on either path. Gradients arrive from the input role and from the output role, they land on the same rows, and they are summed. That is the whole mechanism.

The cited paper's contribution is an account of what that sum contains.

Start untied, where the two gradients can still be looked at separately. Their support is very different.

The input-embedding gradient is nonzero for exactly one row per step: the row of the token currently being fed in. In symbols, $\partial L_t/\partial U_k = 0$ for every $k \neq i_t$. No other row of $U$ hears anything on that step.

The output-embedding gradient touches every row. The target row gets $(p_t(o_t) - 1)h$. Every other row $k$ gets $p_t(k)\,h$, a push scaled by the probability the model wrongly handed that word.

Follow a rare word through training. Its input row moves only on the handful of steps where that word actually appears. Its output row moves on every step of training.

[[tied-embedding-update-dynamics|Tied]], row $S_k$ receives both terms, and the question becomes which of them dominates.

For every row except the current input token, only the output term exists. The update there is exactly the untied output update, with $S$ substituted for $V$.

For the single row where both terms apply, the output term carries a factor of $p_t(i_t)$ — the model's own probability that the current input token is also the next target. Tokens seldom repeat back to back, so that probability is near zero, and the output term at that row is scaled down to almost nothing.

So the input term dominates at the one row it touches, and every other row still moves.

The paper's read is that the tied matrix ends up nearer the untied output embedding than the untied input one. It supports that with rank correlations of pairwise word distances: up to 0.77 for output-versus-tied, and 0.31 to 0.45 for input-versus-tied.

That is the account of the dynamics. The evidence that tying improves quality is a separate thing, and a more indirect one.

Training [[perplexity]] rises while validation and test perplexity fall. The paper reads that pattern as less overfitting, coming from the smaller parameter count.

A failure case is stated too. Tying hurts in skip-gram, where the hidden layer is the identity. There a near-zero $p_t(i_t)$ drives the input row's norm toward zero, with no layer in between to absorb it. Recurrent layers are said to decouple the two roles enough that this does not bite.

Six decoder layers presumably decouple them at least as much. The Transformer does not raise the question.

chapters.title: The translation version, and what it was shown to buy
chapters.body:
The variant the Transformer takes is not the language-model result at all. It is a later section of the same cited paper, the section about translation.

Write out the three matrices involved. The encoder input embedding is $W \in \mathbb{R}^{C_s \times H}$. The decoder holds the same pair as before, $U, V \in \mathbb{R}^{C_t \times H}$. Here $C_s$ is the source vocabulary size and $C_t$ the target vocabulary size.

Decoder-only tying sets $U = V$ and leaves the encoder alone. That is the language-model result carried straight across.

[[three-way-weight-tying|Three-way tying]] goes one step further and sets $W$ equal to them as well. Doing that puts source tokens and target tokens into a single embedding space, sharing rows. It is a substantive claim about the two languages, not just a storage trick.

The cited numbers separate the two rungs.

Decoder-only tying takes a translation model from 168M parameters to 122M.

Three-way takes 165M to 79M on English-German, and 168M to 80M on English-French. That is about 52% off.

Reported BLEU sits within noise of the untied baselines.

Notice what those numbers are and are not evidence for.

The perplexity gain from tying was measured on language models. On translation, the cited result is "half the parameters, same score" — a size claim, and a null result on quality.

[[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing|The Transformer's sharing]] inherits both of those and tests neither.

There is no untied row anywhere in [[transformer-ablations|Table 3]]. Within this paper, then, the choice is never varied against an alternative. [[base-vs-big-transformer|Base and big]] both use it, and the parameter counts reported for each are counts of the already-shared model.

The most one can say from the paper itself is that a model built this way reaches the numbers in [[table-2]]. Whether an untied Transformer would reach them too, at roughly twice the size, is not asked.

chapters.title: One vocabulary, or nothing to share
chapters.body:
Three-way tying carries a prerequisite. Source and target have to index into the same rows. If a token id means one thing on the English side and something else on the German side, there is nothing coherent to share.

[[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] can supply that agreement, but only if the merges are learned the right way.

[[joint-bpe-shared-vocabulary|Joint BPE]] is the variant that supplies it. Concatenate the source and target sides of the training corpus into one pile. Then learn a single ordered list of merges over that pile.

The alternative is to run BPE separately per language. That is more compact, and it guarantees that every subword was seen in text of its own language. But it can segment the same string differently on the two sides.

The cited example is the name Mirzayeva. English splits it Mirz|ayeva. Russian splits it Mir|za|eva. Nothing lines up. The subword-to-subword mapping is harder to learn, and it surfaces as copying and transliteration errors.

Joint merges make the two segmentations agree, because there is only one merge list to replay. The stated cost is small: about 0.05% of test tokens come out as segments that only ever occurred in one language's text.

The overlap that results is not total. At 89,500 joint merges the cited work reports roughly 80K shared subwords out of about 94K for English-German. So "shared vocabulary" means most rows serve both languages and a minority do not.

[[wmt-2014-en-de|The Transformer's English-German setup]] reports the outcome of all of this and none of the procedure. What it gives is one source-target vocabulary of about 37000 tokens.

That figure is downstream of a merge count. [[bpe-vocabulary-size|The vocabulary is the character set plus one symbol per merge]], and the merge count is the only knob the method has. So the 37000 is a chosen number of merges, restated as a total.

[[wmt-2014-en-fr|The English-French model]] is a loose end. It uses a 32000-token [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] vocabulary from a different cited system, and Section 5.1 never calls that vocabulary shared. Section 3.4 states the sharing without listing exceptions, so it presumably still holds. The paper does not confirm it.

chapters.title: The multiplier with no argument
chapters.body:
One clause of Section 3.4 stands on nothing. In the embedding layers, the shared weights are multiplied by $\sqrt{d_{model}}$. At 512 wide, that factor is [[sqrt-dmodel-embedding-multiplier|about 22.6]].

No reason is given. No citation, and no ablation.

Two facts about where the multiplier applies, since the paper never sets them next to each other.

First, the embedding role only. The same matrix is used unscaled when it acts as the output projection. So tying does not force one scale on both jobs after all: the multiplier is what lets those rows be small as logit vectors and large as input vectors at once.

Put another way, it is the only part of the sharing scheme that treats the three roles differently. It is also the part with no stated motive.

Second, the scaled vector's next stop is an addition. [[positional-encoding|Position]] is added to it, not concatenated, and [[eq-posenc|the sinusoids]] have entries in $[-1,1]$ by construction.

That makes the ratio between the two terms the thing that decides how much of the sum is content and how much is order. Multiplying by 22.6 makes the embedding the larger term, for rows of ordinary initialized size.

Then [[residual-dropout|dropout at $P_{drop}=0.1$]] is applied to the sum, in both stacks.

The paper states each of these in a separate sentence, in separate sections, and never puts them side by side.

Compare the model's other square root. Attention divides by [[sqrt-dk-scaling|$\sqrt{d_k}$]], and that division comes with a motive: a suspicion, hedged in the paper as a suspicion, that large dot products push the softmax into small gradients.

This one gets half a sentence.

A reader wanting to know whether 22.6 matters, or whether any constant near it would do, gets nothing here and nothing from [[table-3]].

n-the-argument-in-three-numbers--where-t.title: Where the numbers in the table come from
n-the-argument-in-three-numbers--where-t.intro:
The parent gave you the three numbers. This level does the arithmetic behind them.

Three things to settle. What each count actually multiplies. What the $O(\cdot)$ quietly throws away. And why the second column is a count of waiting rather than a count of work.

It ends on everything the table has no column for.

chapters.title: Counting one self-attention layer
chapters.body:
Start with the shapes. Write the layer's input as a matrix $X$ with $n$ rows, one per position, each row of width $d$. [[queries-keys-values|Queries, keys and values]] are derived from that input, so they are all $n \times d$ as well.

With the shapes fixed, [[eq-attention|the attention equation]] contains exactly two matrix multiplies. Count them one at a time.

The first is $QK^{T}$, which is $(n \times d)$ times $(d \times n)$. The result has $n^2$ entries, one for every ordered pair of positions. Each entry is a dot product of length $d$. So the cost is $n^2 d$ multiply-adds.

The [[softmax]] then runs over those same $n^2$ entries, at constant work each. That is $O(n^2)$, smaller than $n^2 d$ by a factor of $d$. It is dominated by the term before it and dropped.

The second multiply weights the values: $(n \times n)$ times $(n \times d)$. The output has $n \times d$ entries, and each one is a dot product of length $n$. That is $n^2 d$ again.

Add the two multiplies: $2n^2d$. The row reports $O(n^2 \cdot d)$, the constant 2 going the way of every constant.

Now the heads. [[multi-head-attention|Running eight heads]] does not change the entry, and the arithmetic shows why. Each head works at [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = d/h$]] rather than at full width, so each of its two multiplies costs $n^2 d/h$ instead of $n^2 d$. There are $h$ of them. Multiply $n^2 d/h$ by $h$ and you are back at $n^2 d$.

So the row prices single-head and multi-head attention identically. This is the same accounting the paper uses when it says that $h$ narrow heads cost about what one full-width head costs.

That is what the row counts. Now what the row does not carry, which is the projections.

Producing $Q$, $K$ and $V$ from $X$ means three multiplies of shape $(n \times d)(d \times d)$, through [[attention-projection-matrices|the learned matrices]]. Each of those is $O(n \cdot d^2)$. $W^O$ is a fourth of the same shape on the way out.

Written in full, one [[self-attention]] layer is $O(n^2 d + n d^2)$. [[table-1]] reports the first term only. Put another way, the [[complexity-per-layer|complexity column]] is pricing the attention operation, not everything a layer does.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: Counting one recurrent layer
chapters.body:
The recurrent row prices a different shape of computation. Take the layer in its plainest form, $h_t = f(W h_{t-1} + U x_t)$. The state $h_t$ and the input $x_t$ are both of width $d$, and both $W$ and $U$ are $d \times d$.

Count one step. $W h_{t-1}$ is a matrix-vector product, $d^2$ multiply-adds. $U x_t$ is a second one, $d^2$ again. That is $2d^2$, plus $O(d)$ of elementwise work to apply $f$, which the squared term dominates.

There are $n$ steps, one per position. $n$ times $d^2$ gives $O(n \cdot d^2)$.

Two things about that count.

First, nothing in it is quadratic in $n$. A [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent layer]] never forms an object indexed by two positions at once. Position $t$ sees position $t-1$ and nothing else, so there is no $n \times n$ anything to build.

Second, $d$ appears squared for a specific reason. Each step pushes a full-width state through a full-width matrix. That is $d^2$ of work, paid once per position.

The variants people actually use sit inside the constant. An [[lstm]] computes four gate blocks per step; a [[gated-recurrent-unit|GRU]] computes three. Each block carries its own pair of $d \times d$ matrices. A bidirectional layer doubles the whole thing again.

All of that is a factor sitting in front of $n d^2$, and $O(\cdot)$ drops factors. The same goes for the efficiency work the paper cites and then sets aside. [[factorization-tricks]] and [[conditional-computation]] cut that constant, and the paper's line is that the [[sequential-computation-bottleneck|fundamental constraint]] survives them.

So the two rows are not one cost larger than another. They are two different products of the same two numbers: $n \cdot n \cdot d$ on one side, $n \cdot d \cdot d$ on the other.

Which product is smaller depends entirely on which of $n$ and $d$ is bigger. [[complexity-per-layer|The complexity column]] on its own cannot settle that, and [[table-1]] does not say.

chapters.title: The column that counts waiting, not work
chapters.body:
The second column measures the shape of the computation rather than its size. [[minimum-sequential-operations|Minimum sequential operations]] counts the longest chain of steps that must happen strictly in order, as a function of $n$.

Two layers can perform identical arithmetic and still differ here. That is why [[layer-comparison-desiderata|the framework]] carries this as a criterion separate from the first column.

Trace the chain for [[self-attention]]. Project the layer input into $Q$, $K$ and $V$. Multiply $Q$ by $K^{T}$. Apply the [[softmax]]. Multiply by $V$. Project out.

Five steps, and the length of none of them depends on $n$. The chain does not grow with the sequence, because a query at position $i$ is computed from the layer's input at position $i$, never from another position's output. All $n$ rows are ready for the first multiply at the same moment.

For a recurrent layer the chain is the layer's definition. $h_t$ cannot be formed until $h_{t-1}$ exists, and $h_{t-1}$ is waiting on $h_{t-2}$. The chain is $n$ long.

This is the introduction's complaint about recurrence rewritten as a column of [[table-1]] — that positions inside one training example cannot be computed in parallel. Adding GPUs does not shorten a chain.

Two things to hold onto when reading the column.

It counts operations in the abstract, and makes no claim about time on hardware. An $O(1)$ chain of large matrix multiplies can take longer to run than an $O(n)$ chain of small ones.

And it prices one layer. [[n-layers|Six]] stacked layers make the chain six times longer. Six is a constant, and a constant does not move with $n$.

The decoder is not an exception to any of this. Its restriction is applied by [[causal-masking|writing $-\infty$ into forbidden score positions]] inside the same score matrix, before the softmax. Nothing has to run in sequence to enforce it. So [[masked-decoder-self-attention|masked self-attention]] still passes all $n$ positions through together during training.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: Path length is counted in hops through a stack
chapters.body:
The third column's wording matters, so take it literally: the maximum path length between any two input and output positions, in networks composed of the given layer type. Two readings hide in that phrase.

*Maximum* means the worst pair, not the average one. For a sequence of length $n$ the worst pair is the two ends. So the column is asking how far apart the ends of the sentence are.

*Networks composed of* means you count across as many layers as it takes to connect that pair, rather than within a single layer. The number is a property of a stack, not of one layer.

That distinction does no work in the two rows here, since both are settled inside one layer. It does a great deal of work in the rows below them.

For [[self-attention]] the answer is 1, and it stays 1 at any $n$. One [[encoder-self-attention|encoder self-attention]] layer already puts every position into every other position's key set. The two ends are adjacent, whatever the length.

In a [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent layer]] the only route from position 1 to position $n$ runs through the $n-1$ states between them, each one passing the signal along. The count is $n$, and it grows with the sentence.

Now what the column is for. It is about learning, not speed. The paper counts the paths that forward *and* backward signals traverse — the same edges a gradient travels — and its stated reason for caring is that shorter paths make [[long-range-dependencies]] easier to learn.

That reason arrives by citation. Section 4 runs no experiment isolating path length from the other two criteria.

So [[maximum-path-length|the column]] states the paper's most direct case against recurrence while borrowing the premise that makes it matter. [[etheme-case-against-recurrence]] follows that argument end to end.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: What the three columns never price
chapters.body:
Three columns, three asymptotics, and nothing else. Start with the constants every row has swallowed. The gate blocks inside an [[lstm]]. The $h$ projection matrices behind [[multi-head-attention|multi-head attention]]. The six layers of the stack.

The larger omission is structural. [[table-1]] prices one layer of each type. But a Transformer layer is not one row of that table.

Every attention [[sub-layer]] is followed by a [[position-wise-feed-forward-network]]. It expands each position to [[d-ff|$d_{ff} = 2048$]] and projects back down to $d_{model} = 512$, once per position, so that sub-layer costs $O(n \cdot d^2)$ — the same shape as the entire recurrent row. It appears nowhere in the table.

Memory gets no column. The first column counts the $n \times n$ score matrix as arithmetic, which is the cost of computing it. The layer also has to hold it, and hold it again for the backward pass. That storage is quadratic in $n$, where a recurrent layer's stored activations are linear in $n$.

Wall-clock time gets no column either, and the paper's own practical-speed argument lives outside this table. When it picks [[dot-product-attention|dot-product]] over [[additive-attention|additive attention]], it says the two are similar in theoretical complexity, and that the dot product wins in practice because it compiles to optimized matrix-multiply code. An $O(\cdot)$ entry cannot see that difference at all.

Nor is there a column for what the one-hop path costs. [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost|Blending positions into a single weighted average]] loses resolution, and multiple heads are the stated repair. That is a design decision forced by something the [[complexity-per-layer|columns]] do not price.

One last thing about the whole table. No cell in it is a measurement. Section 4 argues about how three quantities scale and offers that as motivation; the experiments arrive later and test something else. [[theme-why-self-attention]] holds the comparison in full.

n-training-the-thing--data-and-vocabular.title: The data, and what the token counts hide
n-training-the-thing--data-and-vocabular.intro:
The level above gave the numbers: 37000, 32000, 25000. This level gives the procedures that produce them.

What the merge loop does, step by step. What happens when that loop meets a word it has never seen before. What the vocabulary size costs in each direction — because it costs something in both directions, and the two costs are not the same shape. And what a batch measured in tokens is actually holding constant.

chapters.title: The merge loop, and what 37000 buys
chapters.body:
The cited procedure starts before any merging happens. Every word in the corpus is written out as a sequence of characters. An end-of-word marker is attached to the last one.

That marker does real work. It keeps a piece that ends a word as a different symbol from the same letters sitting in the middle of a word.

Then the loop begins. Count every adjacent symbol pair across the corpus, weighting each count by how often the word it came from occurs. Find the most frequent pair. Replace every occurrence of that pair with one new symbol. Repeat.

[[bpe-merge-algorithm|The loop]] is greedy and never backtracks — once a merge is made, it stands for the rest of the run. It is Gage's byte-level compression algorithm, with characters standing in where Gage had bytes.

Two things follow from that loop which a merge count alone does not tell you.

The first is about the tail of the word distribution. Frequent words show up in the pair counts often enough to get merged all the way up, and they end as a single symbol. Rare words run out of frequent pairs partway through, and stop as two or three pieces.

The starting character inventory is never removed from the vocabulary as merging proceeds. So there is no cliff at the tail. The segmentation just gets finer as words get rarer. That is why [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] needs no unknown-word token at all.

The second is about size. [[bpe-vocabulary-size|The merge budget]] is a model-size knob as well as a segmentation knob.

Walk the arithmetic. The vocabulary is 37000 rows. Each row is a vector of width [[d-model|$d_{model} = 512$]]. That is $37000 \times 512$, close to 19 million parameters in one table.

And in this model that one table is used three times over. The encoder input embedding, the decoder input embedding, and the pre-softmax output projection are [[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing|one matrix]] — the [[three-way-weight-tying|three-way case]] of the cited work on [[weight-tying|tied embeddings]]. Untied, that would be three separate copies of the 19 million.

The paper adds one wrinkle to the arrangement, and gives no reason for it: in the embedding layers the shared weights are scaled by [[sqrt-dmodel-embedding-multiplier|$\sqrt{d_{model}}$]].

chapters.title: Replaying the list on text you have never seen
chapters.body:
What the merge loop leaves behind is not a lookup table of 37000 strings. It is an ordered list of merge operations. That ordering is the whole of the encoder.

[[bpe-segmentation-at-test-time|To segment any word]], split it into characters. Then replay the merges in the order they were learned, applying each one wherever it fits. No search. No probability model. No fallback branch for the hard cases.

Two properties fall out of that.

The first is consistency. The segmentation of a given string is the same everywhere that string appears. Nothing about the surrounding sentence enters the procedure, so there is nothing for context to change.

The second is what happens in the worst case. A word can survive the entire replay as a string of single characters, with no merge ever firing on it. Every one of those characters is already in the vocabulary, because the starting inventory was never removed.

That is the actual reason there is no unknown token. It is not a claim about how much of the language the vocabulary covers. The one real failure is a character that never appeared in the training corpus at all, which has no symbol to fall back to.

That determinism is what makes [[joint-bpe-shared-vocabulary|joint BPE]] worth the trouble. The merges are learned over both languages' text at once. So an English name and its German copy pass through the same replay and come out as the same pieces.

Put another way: a decoder that has to reproduce or transliterate a string from the source side is copying pieces it can already see on the source side.

The cited work names the catch. Two languages that do not share an alphabet need transliteration first, or the vocabulary is shared in name only. [[wmt-2014-en-de|English and German]] share Latin script, so the paper never has to raise it.

Sharing also changes what the tied table sees during training. [[tied-embedding-update-dynamics|Every row now takes gradient]] from both languages' [[token-embeddings|embedding lookups]], and from every output softmax as well.

chapters.title: The trade, priced in both directions
chapters.body:
[[vocabulary-vs-sequence-length-tradeoff|The trade]] is real, but it is not symmetric. The asymmetry is what makes a middling merge budget the right answer rather than an extreme one.

Take one direction first. Cut the merge count and the vocabulary shrinks: fewer embedding rows to store, and a cheaper output [[softmax]] to compute. Both of those costs are linear in vocabulary size.

Now the other direction. Every sentence lengthens, because with fewer merges available more words break into more pieces. And sequence length is not charged linearly.

A [[self-attention]] layer costs [[complexity-per-layer|$O(n^2 \cdot d)$]] per layer, against a recurrent layer's $O(n \cdot d^2)$ — the comparison [[table-1|laid out row by row]] under Section 4's [[layer-comparison-desiderata|three criteria]].

So the two arms are not interchangeable. The saving from a smaller vocabulary is linear, and it lands in one place: the embedding table and the output projection. The cost is quadratic, and it lands in every attention layer of both stacks.

Section 4's whole cost claim rides on staying on the good side of $n < d$. With $d_{model} = 512$, that condition means sentences of fewer than 512 tokens.

Hedge with the paper here. It says $n < d$ "is most often the case with sentence representations used by state-of-the-art models," and supports that by pointing at word-piece and byte-pair representations. That is a citation, not a measurement.

No length distribution for the WMT corpora is reported anywhere in the paper. The margin is almost certainly large, since subword-split newswire sentences run to tens of tokens rather than hundreds. But the reader is asked to take it rather than shown it.

Where the condition does not hold, the paper offers a plan and not a result. Have each position [[restricted-self-attention|attend only to a neighborhood of size $r$]], and accept a [[maximum-path-length|path length]] of $O(n/r)$ between distant positions in place of a constant one. It is marked as future work. [[theme-why-self-attention]] has the full comparison.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: The other vocabulary, and a sentence the paper does not write
chapters.body:
For [[wmt-2014-en-fr|English-French]] the scheme changes.

[[word-piece-encoding|Word-piece]] is subword tokenization built on the same premise as [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]]: a fixed set of common units, and no out-of-vocabulary token needed. What differs is the rule for picking the units.

BPE merges the pair that occurs most often. [[wordpiece-model|The word-piece model]] from Google's NMT system merges the pair that most improves the likelihood of the training data under a language model over the current units. Frequency against likelihood.

Neither the cited work nor this paper reports a controlled comparison of the two schemes at a fixed vocabulary size. So "32000 word-piece" versus "37000 BPE" is not a result about anything. It is two teams' conventions landing in one experiments section.

There is also something the paper says for one dataset and not for the other. Section 5.1 calls the English-German vocabulary shared between source and target. For English-French it says only that tokens were split into a 32000 word-piece vocabulary. Sharing is not stated.

The one-matrix embedding scheme is described in Section 3.4 as a property of the model rather than of a particular dataset. So the English-French vocabulary is presumably shared too — but the paper does not say it, and the reader has to infer it.

Both vocabularies arrive the same way: by citation, unmodified and unjustified. So does [[adam-optimizer|the optimizer]]. So does [[label-smoothing|the label smoothing]]. So does [[beam-search|the beam search]].

The paper's invention budget goes to the architecture. The rest of [[transformer-training-recipe|the recipe]] is assembled out of other people's defaults, which [[etheme-borrowed-recipe]] tracks piece by piece.

chapters.title: What a token-counted batch holds constant
chapters.body:
[[length-based-batching|Counting a batch in tokens]] rather than in sentences means the number of sentences in a batch is not fixed.

Work it through at roughly 25000 target tokens per batch. A batch made of ten-token sentences holds around 2500 pairs. A batch made of fifty-token sentences holds around 500.

What stays constant across steps is the number of predictions the loss averages over. That count is what the gradient's scale and variance actually depend on. Hold it fixed and one step is comparable to the next.

Grouping sentences by approximate length is not a tidiness preference either. Padding in an attention model is charged at full price: a batch padded to width $n$ costs $n^2$ score computations per example, whether or not the positions in it hold real tokens.

Put a five-token sentence in the same batch as a sixty-token one and the short sentence is padded out to sixty. That is $60^2$ of attention work where $5^2$ was needed — about 144 times what the sentence calls for.

Bucketing keeps the padded width near the true width. So the token count and the work actually done stay roughly proportional.

The two together are what make a step count meaningful. [[training-hardware-and-schedule|100,000 steps]] for the base model, [[warmup-steps-4000|4000 of them warmup]] under [[learning-rate-warmup-schedule|the ramp-and-decay rule]] — all denominated in roughly equal slices of data.

One number the paper does not give: how many passes over the corpus that is. The arithmetic is available anyway, with one assumption bolted on.

100,000 steps at 25000 target tokens each is about 2.5 billion target tokens. The English-German set has 4.5 million sentence pairs; at a plausible thirty target tokens each, one pass over it is roughly 135 million target tokens. So 2.5 billion is on the order of twenty epochs — and about three times that for [[base-vs-big-transformer|the big model]], which runs three times as many steps.

The exact figure depends on token counts the paper never reports. [[tensor2tensor]] is where you would go to recover them.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

n-training-the-thing--three-regularizers.title: Three Regularizers, and Where Each One Acts
n-training-the-thing--three-regularizers.intro:
The parent gave the three settings and their placement. This level gives the machinery underneath them.

Four things, in order. How many masks actually fall in a single forward pass, and what the normalization step sees once they have. A fourth knob that Section 5.4 never lists among its three. The arithmetic behind the one rate that changes between the two model sizes. And the definition of label smoothing, which lives in a cited paper that the Transformer paper applies without restating.

chapters.title: Thirty-two places the mask falls
chapters.body:
Start by counting the sites. Every [[sub-layer]] in the model gets its own mask. An encoder layer holds two sub-layers, so it takes two masks; a decoder layer holds three, so it takes three.

With [[n-layers|$N=6$]] layers in each stack, the count is fixed. Six layers at two masks each is 12 in the [[encoder-stack]]. Six layers at three masks each is 18 in the [[decoder-stack]]. Add the two embedding sums, one on the input side and one on the output side, and a single forward pass applies [[dropout]] in 32 places. All 32 are driven by the single reported rate.

The [[position-wise-feed-forward-network]] gets no special handling in this scheme. It is a sub-layer like any other — wrapped the same way, masked the same way.

Now the order inside the wrapper, which is fixed: compute $\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)$, mask it, add $x$, normalize. What [[layer-normalization]] receives is therefore $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Dropout}(\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)))$. The mask lands on the sub-layer's output only, never on the copy of $x$ carried around it.

Two consequences fall out of that ordering.

First, the worst case is bounded. Suppose a mask happened to zero a sub-layer's entire output. The layer would collapse to $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x)$ — the input, normalized, which is still a usable representation. Gradient would still reach earlier layers, because the [[residual-connection]] path was never touched.

Masking after the addition instead would break exactly that. The identity term would be zeroed along with the sub-layer's contribution, and a whole layer could stop passing signal backwards.

Second, normalization is not the same function at train and test time. It computes a mean and a variance per position, across that position's features. At training time it computes them on a sum whose non-identity half has been thinned by the mask.

So some of the variance the mask removes is absorbed by the rescaling rather than propagating up the stack.

The embedding site is the one with a side effect. [[residual-dropout|Dropout there]] applies to the sum of the [[token-embeddings|token embedding]] and the [[positional-encoding|positional encoding]], not to either of them separately. By the time the mask arrives, [[eq-posenc|the sinusoid vector]] has already been added, and there is only one vector left to mask.

A masked coordinate therefore removes what that token is and where it sits in the same stroke. The order signal has no protected channel of its own.

chapters.title: The knob Section 5.4 does not list
chapters.body:
Section 5.4 opens by saying the paper employs three types of regularization. It then prints two headings: [[residual-dropout]] and [[label-smoothing]].

That leaves a third unaccounted for. It may be the embedding-sum application counted as its own type, or it may be something else. The section does not say.

[[attention-dropout]] appears exactly once in the whole paper, and not in the [[regularization]] section. It surfaces instead in [[constituency-parsing|the parsing experiments]]. There the authors report running a small number of experiments to select "the dropout, both attention and residual", along with learning rates and beam size, on the Section 22 development set.

That sentence points back to 5.4 for a rate that 5.4 never gives.

Two things follow. One: the implementation carries a knob the recipe does not document. Two: the value used for the translation models is never stated.

The parsing section says that everything except those four items stayed unchanged from the English-German base model. That implies a translation-side setting for attention dropout exists. No number is printed for it anywhere.

Placement is also unstated. The site that would make sense in [[eq-attention]] is the softmax output — masking the attention weights before they multiply $V$.

If the mask went there, two things would follow mechanically. A [[attention-head|head]] would lose access to positions it had just selected, and the weights that survived would no longer sum to one.

The paper does not say this. [[scaled-dot-product-attention|The equation]] is given with no dropout term in it.

Where the knob was tuned is the tell. The parsing runs use 40K WSJ sentences, plus a [[semi-supervised-parsing|17M-sentence]] variant, both reported in [[table-4]]. A small-data regime is exactly where a second dropout rate, tunable independently of the first, would be worth the search.

chapters.title: Why one rate moves and the others don't
chapters.body:
Do the arithmetic the rate is tracking. Start with tokens consumed.

[[length-based-batching|Batches hold roughly 25000 target tokens]], and the big models run 300,000 steps — [[training-hardware-and-schedule|3.5 days on 8 P100s]]. Multiply the two: about 7.5 billion target tokens pass through a big-model training run.

Now the size of what is being passed through. [[wmt-2014-en-de]] is 4.5M sentence pairs. At something like 25–30 [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] tokens per sentence, that puts the training set on the order of $10^8$ target tokens.

Divide the one by the other. 7.5 billion tokens consumed against $10^8$ tokens of data is roughly fifty passes over the corpus, for the big English-German model.

[[wmt-2014-en-fr]] is 36M sentences under a [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece vocabulary]], about eight times bigger. The same 300,000 steps consume the same 7.5 billion tokens, so eight times the data puts the count closer to seven passes.

Fifty passes at $P_{drop} = 0.3$. Seven passes at 0.1.

The average sentence length is not reported, so these are order-of-magnitude figures rather than measurements.

They still sharpen the parent's claim. What the rate tracks is not dataset size directly. It is how many times each sentence is seen.

Note that the same logic separates base from big on identical data. The [[base-vs-big-transformer|base model]] runs 100,000 steps instead of 300,000 — a third of the tokens, so on the order of twenty passes — and it stays at 0.1.

The evidence behind this is thinner than the choice.

Rows (C) and (D) of [[table-3]] are the relevant ones. Both are base-size runs, measured on the English-German development set. Section 6.2 reads the result as "as expected, bigger models are better, and dropout is very helpful in avoiding over-fitting" — the ablation confirms a prior rather than discovering anything.

Note what those rows do not cover. None of the table's dropout variations is 0.3, and none is run at big-model size. So [[size-and-dropout-ablation|the row supports the direction, not the number]]. And every entry in [[transformer-ablations|the table]] is a single run.

chapters.title: What the citation actually says
chapters.body:
The paper gives a value and a reference number. It does not restate what the reference says. Here is what the reference contains.

[[label-smoothing-regularization|LSR]] replaces the one-hot target $q$ with a mixture:

$$q'(k) = (1-\epsilon)\,\delta_{k,y} + \epsilon\,u(k)$$

Take $u$ uniform over a vocabulary of size $K$. Then the reference token's target is $1 - \epsilon + \epsilon/K$, and every other token in the vocabulary gets $\epsilon/K$.

Put the paper's numbers in. $\epsilon = 0.1$, and the [[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing|pre-softmax projection]] scores over a vocabulary of roughly 37000 tokens. So $\epsilon/K$ is $0.1/37000$, about $2.7 \times 10^{-6}$, and what is left on the right token is about $0.9$.

That tiny share goes to each of the other 37 thousand tokens — including tokens that could not legally appear there.

[[smoothing-parameter-epsilon|There are two knobs]] here, $\epsilon$ and $u$. And $u$ need not be uniform: the cited work discusses using the corpus prior over classes instead.

The Transformer paper reports only $\epsilon$. Uniform $u$ is an assumption the reader supplies.

[[lsr-as-two-cross-entropy-losses|The loss splits]] in two, because cross entropy is linear in the target:

$$H(q',p) = (1-\epsilon)H(q,p) + \epsilon H(u,p)$$

The first term is the ordinary objective, scaled down. The second is a fixed pull of the predicted distribution toward $u$, equal up to a constant to a KL divergence from $u$.

That second term is identical for every training example. Put another way, it carries nothing that distinguishes one example from another, so there is nothing in it to memorize. That is what makes it a regularizer.

[[overconfidence-and-bounded-logit-gradient|The stated motive]] runs like this. At finite logits the softmax never returns exactly 1, so a one-hot target is only approached as the correct logit runs away from the rest.

The cited argument is that chasing it overfits and leaves the model less able to adapt. That work also notes that the per-logit gradient of the cross entropy is bounded. Smoothing supplies a target with a finite optimum instead of one that keeps receding.

None of this reasoning appears in [[label-smoothing|the paragraph that uses it]]. That paragraph is [[transformer-training-recipe|recipe reporting, not derivation]].

chapters.title: Two metrics pointing opposite ways
chapters.body:
The perplexity loss is close to mechanical. Follow it through.

The model has been trained to put about $0.9$ on the reference token, not $1.0$. [[perplexity]] is the exponentiated mean negative log probability of exactly those reference tokens. Cap the peak and the average NLL rises.

So the paper's phrasing — the model "learns to be more unsure" — describes the objective doing what it was told, not a training failure.

The loss itself now has a floor too. The smoothed cross entropy cannot fall below the entropy of the smoothed target.

[[bleu]] can still improve, because it scores strings rather than probabilities, and the strings come out of [[beam-search]].

Two things determine which strings come out, and neither of them is peak probability. One is which token ranks first at each [[auto-regressive-generation|decoding step]]. The other is how the summed log probabilities of whole hypotheses compare, once [[length-penalty|the length penalty]] has divided them.

A flatter distribution changes the second one. A beam that would have been dominated early by a single confident continuation keeps its alternatives alive longer.

So smoothing can move the tokens actually emitted, while the score on the reference token gets worse.

On evidence: Section 5.4 asserts the whole thing in one sentence, with no numbers attached. It also names a third metric, accuracy, which is never tabulated — not in [[table-2]], not anywhere.

[[table-3]] is where the split is visible. It prints development perplexity and development BLEU in adjacent columns, for every row.

The practical reading: a single-number model-selection criterion would have deleted this regularizer. Tune on held-out perplexity, and smoothing looks like a mistake every time.

n-what-the-numbers-show--one-knob-at-a-t.title: The one place the design is tested
n-what-the-numbers-show--one-knob-at-a-t.intro:
The parent node gave you the rows that matter, and what the paper concluded from them. This level reads the grid as an experiment instead.

An ablation table makes a promise. Change one thing, hold everything else still, and the movement in the result column belongs to the thing you changed. That promise is worth checking block by block.

So three questions run through what follows. What does each block hold fixed? What does it quietly change alongside the knob in its name? And how much of the base configuration does the table actually justify?

chapters.title: What the columns hold fixed
chapters.body:
Start with the shape of the table. [[table-3]] has twelve columns, and they fall into two groups.

Nine columns describe the run. Those are [[n-layers|$N$]], [[d-model|$d_{model}$]], [[d-ff|$d_{ff}$]], [[num-heads-h|$h$]], [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k$ and $d_v$]], the dropout rate $P_{drop}$, the [[label-smoothing|label-smoothing]] value $\epsilon_{ls}$, and the number of training steps. The remaining three report what came out: dev [[perplexity|PPL]], dev [[bleu|BLEU]], and parameter count in millions.

Every ablation row inherits 100K steps, and the same data and decoding setup as the base model. The training budget is therefore constant across the block. Whatever separates two rows, it is not that one of them trained longer.

The parameters column is where the blanks say the most.

Across all four rows of block (A) that cell is empty. The blank is a claim, not an omission. Every row in (A) is built so that $h\,d_k = h\,d_v = 512$: one head at 512, four heads at 128, sixteen at 32, thirty-two at 16. Each of those products comes to 512.

Because the product is pinned, the [[attention-projection-matrices|four projection matrices]] still total $d_{model}\times d_{model}$ however the heads are cut. Nothing is added and nothing is removed. There is no parameter count to print because the parameter count did not move.

Rows (B) are not like that. They print 58 and 60 against the base row's 65. Narrowing $d_k$ while $d_v$ stays fixed genuinely deletes weights from $W^Q$ and $W^K$, and the column records it. A knob-name and a controlled comparison are not the same thing here.

One more feature of the grid before the blocks themselves. The last row is not an ablation at all.

It is the [[base-vs-big-transformer|big model]]: 1024 wide, $d_{ff}$ of 4096, sixteen heads, $P_{drop}=0.3$, 300K steps. It reports 4.33 PPL and 26.4 BLEU at 213M parameters. Every (C) knob it touches, it takes at the winning end.

So the table is doing two jobs at once. It diagnoses the base model, and it shows where the configuration behind [[table-2]] came from.

chapters.title: Four head counts, read with the perplexity column
chapters.body:
The parent gave you the BLEU column for this sweep. The perplexity column runs alongside it, and it orders the four settings the same way.

Read it across: 5.29 at one head, 5.00 at four, 4.92 at eight, 4.91 at sixteen, 5.01 at thirty-two. Two metrics agreeing on an ordering is worth something.

But note where the minimum sits. Sixteen heads post the lowest perplexity of any row in the ablation block. The base row, at eight heads, does not win its own sweep on either metric.

The single-head row also carries a second change alongside the head count. With $h=1$, the fixed product $h\,d_k = h\,d_v = 512$ forces [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = 512$]]. So the worst row in (A) is also the row with the widest keys and values in the entire table.

That is the shape the paper wants, because its argument for [[multi-head-attention|multi-head attention]] in [[eq-multihead|Equation (2)]] is not an argument about dimension. It is an argument about what a single attention operation does to information: it collapses many positions into one weighted average, and [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost|averaging can blur what was specific to the individual positions]]. Put another way, once the sum is taken, what each position contributed to it is no longer separable.

Rows (A) are consistent with that story. They do not test it. Nothing here shows heads occupying different subspaces — that is left to the hand-picked patterns in [[fig-5]] and to the hedged claim about [[attention-interpretability|individual heads appearing to learn distinct roles]].

So take [[attention-heads-ablation|the sweep]] for the one thing it licenses cleanly. At fixed compute, one head is worse than several, by 0.9 BLEU against the best setting.

It does not license $h=8$ over $h=16$. That gap is 0.1 BLEU, on one training run each, with no seeds and no variance reported anywhere in the paper.

chapters.title: What rows (B) actually shrank
chapters.body:
[[key-size-ablation|Rows (B)]] leave the rest of the head configuration alone. Both rows hold $h=8$ and $d_v=64$, and cut only $d_k$.

At $d_k=32$: 5.01 PPL and 25.4 BLEU. At $d_k=16$: 5.16 and 25.1. Perplexity rises as BLEU falls, so both directions of the metric agree that the cut hurts.

That is what the row says. Now what else moved under the label.

Two things travel with that single number. The first is capacity. Parameters fall to 60M and then 58M, because [[attention-projection-matrices|$W^Q$ and $W^K$]] narrow while $W^V$ and $W^O$ stay the size they were. A small capacity loss rides along with the knob.

The second is the layer's total key width. Summed across the eight heads, $h\,d_k$ drops from 512 to 256, and then to 128. Every row of (A), by construction, held that sum at 512.

That second change is what limits how far the finding generalizes. The table already contains another configuration with a per-head $d_k$ of 32 — the sixteen-head row of (A) — and it scores 25.8. So a per-head key size of 32 is not damaging on its own. What (B) removes is the layer's total budget for computing matches.

The paper's own gloss goes elsewhere. It says that determining compatibility is not easy, and that a more sophisticated [[compatibility-function]] than [[dot-product-attention|a dot product]] may be beneficial. That is a hypothesis, stated once and then dropped. [[additive-attention]] is the obvious candidate for such a function, and Section 3.2.1 had already set it aside — on speed, not on quality.

There is also a small tension worth naming. [[sqrt-dk-scaling|The $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor]] in [[eq-attention|Equation (1)]] exists because dot products grow unmanageably large as $d_k$ grows. That is a repair applied at the large end of the range. Rows (B) show the small end underperforming. So [[scaled-dot-product-attention]] is patched where $d_k$ is big and weak where $d_k$ is small.

chapters.title: Rows (C) and (D): where the BLEU is bought
chapters.body:
[[size-and-dropout-ablation|Rows (C)]] are seven rows, not one finding. Depth first.

[[n-layers|$N$]] of 2 gives 23.7 BLEU at 36M parameters. $N$ of 4 gives 25.3 at 50M. $N$ of 8 gives 25.5 at 80M — and 4.88 PPL, which is better than the base row, while its BLEU sits 0.3 below the base. "Bigger is better" holds in aggregate and breaks at the margin.

Width is the more useful half. Cutting [[d-model|$d_{model}$]] to 256 costs 1.3 BLEU and saves 37M parameters. Raising it to 1024 buys 26.0 BLEU for 168M.

Now set that against widening only [[d-ff|the feed-forward inner layer]]. With $d_{ff}$ at 4096, the row scores 26.2 BLEU at 90M parameters. That is the best ablation row in the table. Nearly half the parameters of the 1024-wide row, and slightly more BLEU.

If the table says anything about where to spend, it says the [[position-wise-feed-forward-network]] is the cheaper axis. The paper does not comment on it.

Rows (D) vary two regularizers, and the two behave differently.

Take [[residual-dropout|dropout]] first. At 0.0 the model gives 5.77 PPL and 24.6 BLEU. At 0.2 it gives 4.95 and 25.5. The base value of 0.1 beats both, so it is an interior optimum — worse on either side of it.

[[label-smoothing]] is stranger. At $\epsilon_{ls}=0.0$ the model records 4.67 [[perplexity|PPL]], the best of any ablation row, with [[bleu|BLEU]] down at 25.3. At $\epsilon_{ls}=0.2$ perplexity degrades to 5.47, while BLEU holds at 25.7.

The two result columns move in opposite directions here. That is Section 5.4's claim printed as data: [[label-smoothing-regularization|smoothing]] makes the model less sure of its predictions, and it scores better anyway.

Put another way, the two columns cannot be read as one axis. A row that assigns higher probability to the reference tokens is not thereby a row that translates better.

chapters.title: Row (E), and how much any of this weighs
chapters.body:
Row (E) is the only row whose cells are a sentence rather than numbers: a positional embedding in place of the sinusoids. It reports 4.92 PPL and 25.7 BLEU. The perplexity matches the base row to two decimals, and the BLEU is 0.1 under it.

The paper calls the two nearly identical. Then it keeps [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding|the sinusoids]] of [[eq-posenc|Equation (4)]] anyway.

The reason it gives is not in this table. It is an untested argument: that fixed encodings may extrapolate to sequence lengths beyond those seen in training, and that [[relative-position-linearity|for any fixed offset the encoding stays a linear function of the position it is offset from]].

So the choice of [[positional-encoding]] is settled somewhere other than here. Row (E) establishes something narrower. It establishes that [[learned-positional-embedding|the alternative]] costs nothing measurable at these lengths.

That is the right note to end on, because the caption limits what any row can carry.

The perplexities are per word-piece, under the paper's [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] vocabulary. The caption uses the word-piece term for a BPE segmentation, and either way the figures index against a 37000-token subword inventory. They are an internal ordering within this table and nothing else. See [[word-piece-encoding]] for the other scheme in play.

All the numbers are newstest2013. That is the development set — and it is the same set on which [[beam-search|the beam size and $\alpha$]] were themselves chosen.

[[checkpoint-averaging]] is off for these runs. So every row here sits below the setup that produced [[table-2]], by construction.

And each row is one training run.

Under that constraint, the differences the table can actually support are the large ones: one head, two layers, no dropout, $d_{model}=256$. The 0.1s and 0.3s are not readable.

n-the-shape-of-the-model--add-then-norma.title: Why This Normalizer and Not the Other
n-the-shape-of-the-model--add-then-norma.intro:
The parent gave the verdict. This level does the arithmetic underneath it.

Four things get worked out here. First, which sums each normalizer actually takes, and along which axis. Second, what a training batch in this particular setup contains, counted in sentences rather than in tokens. Third, what is left of a batch once decoding starts and beam search is running. Fourth, what the invariance results say once they are written out rather than gestured at.

chapters.title: Same recipe, different axis
chapters.body:
Start with what the two normalizers have in common, because it is most of the operation. Both do the same three things. Subtract a mean, divide by a standard deviation, then apply a learned per-unit gain and bias.

They differ in one axis. That is the whole of the difference: the two sums that produce the mean and the standard deviation run over different things.

Take the output of one [[sub-layer]] as a tensor with three axes — sentences in the batch, positions within a sentence, units within a vector. [[layer-norm-vs-batch-norm|Batch normalization]] fixes a unit and a position, then averages down the sentence axis. That gives one mean and one variance per (unit, position) pair. [[layer-normalization-statistics|Layer normalization]] fixes a sentence and a position instead, and averages along the unit axis:

$$\mu=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{i=1}^{H}a_i,\qquad \sigma=\sqrt{\frac{1}{H}\sum_{i=1}^{H}(a_i-\mu)^2}$$

with $H$ the number of units. In this model $H$ is [[d-model|512]] at every normalizer. It is 512 everywhere because every sub-layer and embedding layer is built to that one width, which is what makes the [[residual-connection|residual additions]] line up. Each of the six [[encoder-stack|encoder]] layers normalizes $x+\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)$ twice. Each [[decoder-stack|decoder]] layer does it three times.

That is the structure. Now what follows from it.

The sample size behind the estimate is a constant here. Every mean in the model is an average of exactly 512 numbers. In the first layer and in the sixth. At position 1 and at position 200. During training and during decoding.

A batch-norm estimate at a given position would instead average over however many sentences reached that position. That count is not fixed by the architecture.

The [[gain-and-bias-parameters|gain and bias]] follow the same pattern. There is one pair per unit, [[per-timestep-normalization|shared across positions]] rather than learned separately at each one. So the normalizer's parameter count does not depend on sequence length either.

chapters.title: What one batch here actually holds
chapters.body:
The packing sets the divisor. A training batch here is about 25000 source tokens and about 25000 target tokens, [[length-based-batching|assembled from sentence pairs of similar length]]. It is sized in tokens rather than in sentences because tokens are what keeps per-step compute even. The number of sentences is whatever falls out of that.

Work the count. WMT 2014 English-German is 4.5M sentence pairs, segmented by [[byte-pair-encoding|byte-pair encoding]] into a shared vocabulary of about 37000 tokens. A batch of short pairs, at roughly 25 tokens a side, holds on the order of a thousand of them. A batch drawn from the long tail, at roughly 100 tokens a side, holds about a quarter as many.

A [[layer-norm-vs-batch-norm|batch statistic]] at position $t$ would be an average over that count. And the count moves by several times across a run.

The length sorting cuts both ways, and both directions matter.

One direction hurts. The batches with the fewest sentences are exactly the batches of longest sentences. So the positions needing the most samples sit where there are fewest sentences to draw them from.

The other direction helps. Sentences within a batch end at nearly the same place, so late positions are not starved the way they would be under random batching, where a handful of unusually long sentences would carry the estimate alone. The dependence is smoothed, not removed.

There is a bookkeeping point too. [[self-attention|Every position of a sentence is computed at once]] here, so a batch is a padded rectangle. A sum down the sentence axis therefore has to exclude the padded slots by hand, or it averages zeros in with real activations. [[per-timestep-normalization|A sum across the 512 units of one real position]] never meets a padded slot at all.

None of this reasoning is in this paper. It is the cited argument applied to this [[transformer-training-recipe|recipe]].

chapters.title: At decode time there is no batch
chapters.body:
Training is only half of it.

Batch normalization has no batch at test time. So it carries stored running estimates, computed during training and reused later. In a sequence model those estimates are indexed by position as well as by unit — one table entry per (unit, position) pair.

That indexing meets the decoding rule. This decoder caps output at [[inference-length-limit|input length plus 50 tokens]], so a long input can be decoded past any position the stored table saw in training. Estimates for those positions would have to be extrapolated, or borrowed from a neighbour.

What batch dimension does exist during decoding is the hypothesis set. The paper decodes with [[beam-search|beam search]] at beam size 4, under a [[length-penalty|length penalty of $\alpha = 0.6$]], and terminates hypotheses early where it can. So the number of live sequences moving through the stack changes from step to step. That number has nothing to do with the training distribution. [[auto-regressive-generation|One generation step]] extends each live hypothesis by one position, through the whole [[decoder-stack|decoder]].

Then there is [[checkpoint-averaging|checkpoint averaging]]. The reported models are not single checkpoints. Base results average the last 5 checkpoints, written at 10-minute intervals; big results average the last 20.

Averaging weights elementwise is well defined — the mean of several weights is a weight. What a pair of running mean and variance tables should become under that same average is a further decision. Someone would have to make it and report it.

[[per-timestep-normalization|Normalizing within a position]] leaves none of that open. There is no stored state. Nothing is estimated during training and reused later. It is the same function of the same 512 numbers whether the position sits in a full training batch or in the third of four surviving beams.

chapters.title: The invariance results, spelled out
chapters.body:
The cited paper's second argument is about geometry rather than batches.

Set it up first. Write a unit's pre-activation as a row of $W$ dotted with the input.

Now scale the whole matrix, $W \to \delta W$. Every pre-activation scales by $\delta$. So $\mu$ scales by $\delta$, and $\sigma$ scales by $\delta$ with it. The ratio $(a-\mu)/\sigma$ therefore comes out unchanged.

Now the shift instead. Add the same vector to every row, and every pre-activation gains the same scalar. [[layer-normalization-statistics|Subtracting the mean across units]] removes it. Those are the two [[normalization-invariance-properties|whole-matrix invariances]].

The complement is worth stating, because it is where the two normalizers separate rather than agree.

Re-scale one unit's incoming weight vector alone, leaving the rest of $W$ untouched. Layer norm is not invariant to that. That unit's pre-activation moves, the across-unit mean and variance move with it, and so every unit's normalized output changes, not only the one that was touched. [[layer-norm-vs-batch-norm|Batch normalization]] absorbs exactly that case, since it normalizes each unit on its own. The trade runs the other way too: layer norm is instead invariant to re-scaling a single training case, which batch norm is not.

The step-size claim follows from the first invariance. If the output is unchanged under $W \to \delta W$, the gradient with respect to the scaled weights carries a factor $1/\delta$. Put another way: as a layer's weights grow, its updates shrink in proportion, and the schedule is never told that this is happening. That is the mechanism the cited work offers for faster convergence.

Standardization also costs something. Each position's vector is pinned to mean zero and norm $\sqrt{512}$. Scale and offset therefore stop carrying information, because they are fixed by construction rather than free to vary with the input.

The [[gain-and-bias-parameters|learned gain and bias]] give them back, one pair per unit, applied before the non-linearity in the cited formulation — and [[layer-normalization]] is not invariant to re-scaling them.

chapters.title: Why the speed claim could not be isolated here
chapters.body:
Suppose you did want to check the faster-training claim on this model. Two other parts of the recipe already control step size.

The first is the schedule. The [[learning-rate-warmup-schedule|warmup schedule]] makes the rate [[eq-lrate|a function of the step number]]: a linear ramp for [[warmup-steps-4000|4000 steps]], then inverse-square-root decay after that.

The second is the optimizer. [[adam-optimizer|Adam]] rescales every parameter by its own running second-moment estimate, run here with [[transformer-adam-settings|$\beta_2 = 0.98$]], below the usual default.

Both of those shrink effective steps as training runs. The [[normalization-invariance-properties|invariance argument]] says the normalizer shrinks them too, in proportion to weight norm. A measurement would see all three at once.

[[table-3|The ablation table]] shows what the authors did vary one knob at a time. Head count and key dimension at fixed compute. $d_k$ on its own. Model size. Dropout rate. Sinusoidal against learned positional encodings. [[transformer-ablations|Five groups of rows]] — none for the normalizer, and none for the wrapper it sits in.

The numbers that reach [[table-2]] are 28.4 BLEU English-German, 41.0 English-French, [[training-hardware-and-schedule|3.5 days on eight P100s]]. Those are evidence for the recipe as a whole.

So the position to hold is narrow. This paper cites [[layer-normalization]] and states where it goes in the stack. The case for it, batch statistics and invariances alike, lives in [[layer-normalization-statistics|the cited paper]]. And it was argued there about recurrent networks, rather than about this architecture.
