n-three-wirings-of-the-same-block--all-p.title: Six rounds, and what the stack carries forward
n-three-wirings-of-the-same-block--all-p.intro:
The parent gave the wrapper as a formula. A formula is a compact object, and this level opens it up.

Five things to open. What layer normalization actually computes. Where dropout sits inside the wrapper. What the residual addition forces on every other width in the model. How much of an encoder layer the feed-forward block really is. And how thin the evidence is that position survives the climb.

chapters.title: Inside the Add & Norm box
chapters.body:
The paper writes $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$ and stops there. [[layer-normalization]] arrives by citation. The formula for it never appears in this paper at all.

So the definition has to come from the cited work. Take one position's 512 activations. Compute their mean and standard deviation *across those 512 units*. Standardize by those two statistics. Then apply a learned gain and a learned bias, one of each per unit ([[layer-normalization-statistics]], [[gain-and-bias-parameters]]).

The detail that matters is where the statistics come from. They come from a single position's own features. They never come from the batch.

That is what makes the operation usable here. [[layer-norm-vs-batch-norm|Batch normalization]] computes each unit's statistics across the examples in a mini-batch instead. When those examples are sentences of different lengths, that is awkward. [[per-timestep-normalization|Normalizing independently at each step]], using only that step's activations, is the property the cited paper claims for sequence models specifically.

The cited work also makes a further argument. Normalizing this way makes the layer invariant to rescaling its whole weight matrix, and it changes the effective learning rate ([[normalization-invariance-properties]]). This paper does not repeat that argument. It does not test it either.

Now the ordering, which is easy to skim past. The addition comes first and the normalization comes second. So the thing being standardized is the residual sum, not the sub-layer's output on its own.

Follow what that does to the identity path. The input $x$ is renormalized every time it passes through a wrapper. It is not carried through untouched. The paper does not discuss the alternative ordering.

One piece of the wrapper is missing from Section 3.1 and only turns up in Section 5.4. Dropout is applied to each [[sub-layer]]'s output *before* the addition.

So at training time the wrapper is $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Dropout}(\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)))$, at [[residual-dropout|$P_{drop} = 0.1$]] for the base model. Note which of the two terms the dropout sits on. The [[residual-connection|identity term]] is never dropped; only the increment is.

Group (D) of [[table-3]] puts the cost of removing it at 1.2 BLEU.

chapters.title: The width the addition forces
chapters.body:
Start with the addition itself. $x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x)$ is elementwise. Two vectors added elementwise must have the same shape, so a sub-layer's output has to match its own input, width for width.

Section 3.1 states the consequence in one sentence: to facilitate the residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension [[d-model|$d_{model} = 512$]].

Read as written, that sentence sounds like a specification — a number someone picked. It is a constraint. And it propagates outward to everything the addition touches.

Take the pieces one at a time. [[multi-head-attention]] may split its work however it likes internally, but its concatenated output has to land back on 512. That is why, with [[num-heads-h|$h = 8$]] heads, the paper sets [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = 512/8 = 64$]]. Divide 512 across 8 heads and each head gets 64 dimensions. The eight head outputs then already sum to 512 before $W^O$ acts on them.

[[token-embeddings|Embeddings]] must be 512 for the same reason — their output feeds the first addition. And because one matrix serves as both the embedding table and the pre-softmax projection ([[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing]]), that matrix is pinned to 512 too.

[[positional-encoding]] is summed with the embeddings rather than concatenated onto them. Summing is elementwise. So the positional vectors are 512 wide as well.

That leaves exactly one width free. The feed-forward block's inner 2048 is the only dimension inside an encoder layer allowed to differ, and only because the block comes back down to 512 before the add.

That is the constraint. Now what it costs.

Width is not a per-layer knob. Group (C) of [[table-3]] can only move $d_{model}$ as a single number for the entire model. Setting it to 256 loses 1.3 BLEU. Setting it to 1024 gains 0.2 BLEU, and takes the parameter count from 65M to 168M ([[size-and-dropout-ablation]]).

There is no row in the table that narrows a late layer or widens an early one. The architecture has no way to express such a model. [[fig-1]] draws one arrow width throughout for exactly this reason.

chapters.title: Where the encoder's weights actually are
chapters.body:
The parent gave the formula. What it did not say is how much of an encoder layer this block actually is. That is a counting question, so count.

Per layer, [[eq-ffn|the two matrices]] are $512 \times 2048$ and $2048 \times 512$. Each holds a little over a million entries. Together, with their biases, that is about 2.1M parameters.

The attention sub-layer sitting beside it holds four projections, each $512 \times 512$ — [[attention-projection-matrices|$W^Q, W^K, W^V, W^O$]]. Four matrices of $512 \times 512$ come to about 1.05M.

So inside one encoder layer the split is roughly two to one. Roughly two thirds of every encoder layer sits in the part that never looks at another position.

Six layers of that is about 12.6M, out of the encoder's ~19M. This is arithmetic worked out here from the paper's stated numbers. The paper never breaks the count down itself.

[[d-ff|2048]] is four times [[d-model|512]], and the paper gives no argument for that ratio. It does test it.

Group (C) of [[table-3]] tries 1024 and 4096 in place of 2048. Those runs get 25.4 and 26.2 BLEU, against the base model's 25.8.

That 26.2 is worth sitting with. It is the best figure any base-depth variant in the table reaches. It is ahead of the row that doubles $d_{model}$, and it gets there at 90M parameters against that row's 168M.

The paper reports it under the heading that bigger models are better. It keeps 2048 anyway.

The [[relu]] between the two matrices is the only nonlinearity in an encoder layer outside the attention softmax.

Consider dropping it. Two linear maps in sequence compose into a single linear map, so $512 \to 2048 \to 512$ would collapse into one $512 \to 512$ linear. What is left in the layer is weighted averaging and affine maps.

The paper offers an alternative reading of the same block: two convolutions of kernel size 1. That is the same arithmetic, described in the vocabulary of [[convolutional-sequence-models|the convolutional models]] this architecture is displacing.

[[position-wise-feed-forward-network|The block's own page]] works through the sharing rules.

chapters.title: What position has to survive
chapters.body:
Injected once, at the bottom — the parent said that. The part it left out is scale.

Two numbers set that scale. Section 3.4 multiplies the embedding weights by [[sqrt-dmodel-embedding-multiplier|$\sqrt{d_{model}} \approx 22.6$]]. And [[eq-posenc|the sinusoids]] have entries bounded in $[-1, 1]$, because sine and cosine cannot leave that range.

Put the two side by side. The content vectors have been scaled up by roughly 22.6. The order signal is capped at 1 in every dimension. When the two are summed, the order signal is small next to the content it rides on.

That sum then passes through dropout at 0.1, in both stacks ([[residual-dropout]], Section 5.4). Put another way: a tenth of an already-small order signal is zeroed before layer 1 has seen any of it.

The paper states both facts, the multiplier and the dropout, in separate sections. It never puts them together.

After that, nothing re-injects position. Every later [[sub-layer]] can only move order information forward along the residual path. And every attention sub-layer that touches it does so by averaging over positions with softmax weights.

That is the setup. On whether the signal holds up through the climb, the paper offers nothing direct.

Row (E) of [[table-3]] does swap [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding|sinusoids]] for [[learned-positional-embedding|learned positional embeddings]]. It reports 4.92 PPL and 25.7 BLEU, against the base model's 4.92 and 25.8.

Read carefully what those near-identical numbers show. They are evidence that the two encodings are interchangeable. They are not evidence that either one reaches layer 6 intact.

The stated reasons for keeping sinusoids are two. The first is a hypothesis: for any fixed offset, [[relative-position-linearity|the encoding of the shifted position is a linear function of the encoding of the original]], so attending by relative position should be easy to learn. The second is a "may" about extrapolating to sequence lengths longer than those seen in training.

Neither is tested. The frequency argument behind the sinusoids is worked out on [[positional-encoding|the encoding's page]].

n-three-wirings-of-the-same-block--all-p.title: The only layer the paper opens
n-three-wirings-of-the-same-block--all-p.intro:
The parent said what the three appendix pictures show. This level is about how they are drawn, and about what that way of drawing can and cannot carry.

Four things, in order. The encoding itself: what a line on the page stands for. What each figure has to throw away in order to stay legible. What the choice of layer 5 leaves unexamined. And the one measured statement about heads in the paper, in Table 3, which does not line up with the pictures.

chapters.title: One drawing convention, three pictures
chapters.body:
Start with the drawing convention. All three panels use the same one, and pinning it down is what bounds everything that can be read off them.

Each panel prints the sentence twice, once along the top and once along the bottom. The top copy holds the querying positions. The bottom copy holds the positions being attended to.

The two copies are identical, and that is not a stylistic choice. This is [[encoder-self-attention]], where the [[queries-keys-values|queries, keys and values]] all come from the same place: the layer below. One sequence plays both roles, so the row you query from and the row you attend to are the same row of tokens.

A line drawn from a top token to a bottom token is one attention weight. Its opacity is that weight's only representation on the page. There is no axis, no tick, no printed number.

Now what that weight is. The weights leaving any one query are a [[softmax]] output, so they sum to 1 across every bottom position — every position, without exception. In [[fig-3]] that means the sum runs over 33 slots. Those 33 include `<EOS>` and six `<pad>`. Padding is not excluded from the distribution; it sits inside it and takes weight like anything else.

Two consequences follow, and both limit what the pictures can be used for.

The first is about comparison. Because each query's weights are normalized on their own, a line's darkness is interpretable only against the other lines leaving that same query in that same head. Comparing one head's opacity to another's, or one query's to another's, or one figure's to another's, is eyeballing.

The second is about absence. A head that spreads its 1.0 thinly over thirty positions gives each of them about a thirtieth of the mass, and thirty lines that faint disappear into the page. So a line you cannot see is not a weight of zero. It may be a small weight drawn too faint to survive printing.

Figure 3 softens the second problem a little with the colored strip printed under its bottom sentence: one row per [[attention-head|head]], one column per word, shade for weight. That strip shows the same numbers the lines do, laid out where nothing can hide behind anything else. It still carries no scale.

One more thing the encoding does not do. Color in these figures identifies which head drew a line. It never encodes how much.

That matters because of how many heads are running. With [[num-heads-h|eight]] heads live at once, a complete map of one query is eight overlaid distributions, and a complete map of the sentence is that, times every query in it.

Nothing on a page can hold that. So each figure throws something away to stay legible. Figure 3 keeps one query. [[fig-4]] keeps one word. [[fig-5]] keeps one head per panel. Full [[multi-head-attention]] on a whole sentence is never drawn anywhere in the paper.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: One query row, and what it is evidence for
chapters.body:
[[fig-3]] is placed where it is for a reason, and the reason is not that it says something new about heads. It is there to make an earlier argument concrete.

That argument is about distance. In the sentence, "making" and "difficult" are seven tokens apart.

Consider what that distance costs in a [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent]] encoder. The forward signal from one to the other has to pass through seven successive steps of hidden state. On the backward pass, the gradient has to make the same seven-step trip in reverse.

Here it is one dot product. Query at "making", key at "difficult", one operation, regardless of the gap. That constant is the [[maximum-path-length]] that [[table-1]] tabulates, and it is the third of Section 4's [[layer-comparison-desiderata|three criteria]] rendered as a single picture.

That is the intended reading. Look at which heads actually land where, and the tidy version loosens.

Four colors converge on "more" and four converge on "difficult". Two of them — blue and green — appear in both groups. So a head is not one target and one job; the same head is sending weight to more than one place.

Other heads are harder to fit to the story at all. A purple head sends weight back to "making" itself, a self-link, which carries no dependency between positions whatsoever. A pink head goes to "2009" and "laws", which are not the verb's complement and are not what the caption is about. What those heads are doing is not addressed anywhere in the paper.

The deeper caveat is not about which head goes where. It is about the layer.

This is layer 5 of [[n-layers|six]] in the [[encoder-stack]]. It is not the embedding layer. The vector doing the querying at the "making" slot has already passed through four rounds of all-pairs mixing, plus the four feed-forward blocks that sit between them.

So that vector is not the word "making". It is a mixture of the whole sentence that happens to be carried in the slot where "making" went in.

Put another way: "making attends to difficult" is shorthand. What the picture shows is a relation between two positions whose contents have already been blended with everything else. The figure supports the [[long-range-dependencies|long-distance]] claim by example. It does not isolate the word.

chapters.title: Sharpness, and the panel that gets discarded
chapters.body:
[[fig-4]] has two panels, and the top one is there to be discarded.

That top panel is head 5's complete map over the sentence — every query, every target. It is mostly a haze of faint lines with a few dark ones in it. It is shown, and then it is set aside.

The bottom panel does the actual work, and it does it by deleting. Everything goes except the lines leaving the single word "its". Only with the rest of the map gone can you see head 5 going almost entirely to "Law" and head 6 going almost entirely to "application".

So the readable claim exists because of a filter the authors chose: this one word, and these two heads out of eight. That is what the "apparently" in the caption is doing.

That is the framing. Now the part that is genuinely notable, which is the sharpness the caption flags.

A near-one-hot distribution at layer 5 is not something the architecture asks for. There is no sparsity penalty in the loss. There is no temperature knob to sharpen the softmax.

If anything the machinery pushes the other way. The $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ divisor in [[scaled-dot-product-attention|Equation 1]] is there precisely to stop the softmax from saturating, and [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k=64$]] bounds how large the logits usually get in the first place.

So concentration on one position is a learned outcome, not a designed one. It is also the one property of these plots you can judge without comparing across heads, since it is visible inside a single query's own set of lines.

One more thing about where that behavior came from. The training signal is [[machine-translation]] alone. No annotation of any kind, anywhere in the setup, names an antecedent for a pronoun.

The paper does not go further than the observation, and neither should the reader. This is one pronoun, in one sentence, offered as an illustration of [[attention-interpretability|what inspecting the distributions suggests]] — with the hedge in the caption doing the load-bearing work.

No count is given for how often heads 5 and 6 split this way. None is given for whether they do it on any other sentence at all.

chapters.title: What layer 5 leaves unexamined
chapters.body:
[[fig-5]] drops the filtering. It shows two complete maps, unedited. That makes it the strongest visual claim in the appendix, and also the loosest.

The two maps do not look alike. The green head is diffuse: a faint wash over nearly every pair of positions, with heavy fans converging on "Law", "application", "missing" and "opinion". The red head is sparse and short-range, most of its queries picking out one or two nearby tokens and little else.

Same sentence, same layer, same trained model. Everything is held fixed except which head you are looking at, so the difference is the heads.

One detail cuts against reading too much into either panel. Both of them carry a dark self-link on `<pad>`. A [[softmax]] has to put its mass somewhere, and a padding slot is a legal place to put it. Not every heavy line on these pages is linguistic.

That is what the figures show. Now the scope of what they cover.

All three figures come from layer 5. Layers 1 through 4 are never shown, and neither is layer 6. So nothing here indicates whether this behavior develops gradually with depth, or whether it is peculiar to one place in the [[encoder-stack|stack]].

The gap in wiring is wider still. Neither [[masked-decoder-self-attention]] nor [[encoder-decoder-attention]] appears in the appendix at all. Those are two of the three wirings [[multi-head-attention|the block]] is used in, and neither is ever pictured.

Add up the evidence base. Two sentences, both English. One trained model. No parse annotation to check any of it against. No tally over a corpus.

So the licensed claim is existence: these heads, on these sentences, did this. It is not a claim about frequency. It is not a claim about reliability. It is not a claim that any head does this in general.

Section 4's wording matches that scope. [[attention-interpretability|Interpretability]] is filed there as a side benefit rather than a result, and the heads are said to "appear to exhibit" behavior related to structure.

Figure 5's caption splits along the same seam. It states flatly that the two heads learned different tasks. It hedges only the tie between those tasks and syntactic structure.

And Section 4's actual argument for the swap does not rest here. It rests on the counts — [[theme-why-self-attention|complexity, parallelism and path length]].

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: The one measured claim, and what it misses
chapters.body:
[[table-3]] rows (A) are the only place in the paper where heads are tested rather than illustrated.

The sweep is set up to hold total computation fixed. It does that by setting $d_k=d_v=d_{model}/h$, so the head width falls as the head count rises.

Work the arithmetic through. $d_{model}$ is 512. With one head, that head gets all 512 dimensions. With [[num-heads-h|$h$]] at 8, each head gets $512/8 = 64$. Push to 32 heads and each one is down to $512/32 = 16$.

The results move with that. Single-head attention, at $d_k=512$, gives 5.29 [[perplexity|PPL]] and 24.9 [[bleu|BLEU]]. At $h=8$ it is 4.92 and 25.8. At $h=16$ it is 4.91 and 25.8. At $h=32$, with $d_k=16$, BLEU falls back to 25.4.

So the curve is flat across the middle and worse at both ends. From the single head to the best setting is $25.8 - 24.9$, which is [[attention-heads-ablation|0.9 BLEU between one head and the best]].

That is the number. The sweep that produced it is not clean.

The reason is in the setup. Head count and head width move together by construction — you cannot add heads in this table without narrowing them. And rows (B) show separately that [[key-size-ablation|cutting $d_k$ on its own hurts]].

So the drop at 32 heads has two candidate causes: too many heads, or 16-dimensional keys. Both rows are reported. The paper does not reconcile them.

The smaller print matters too. Each row is a single training run, scored on newstest2013, and its perplexity is per wordpiece — a figure that does not travel outside this paper's own tokenization.

What the number does support is narrow. Several heads beat one head. That attaches a value to the [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost|averaging argument]] of Section 3.2.2, and that is all it does.

It says nothing about specialization. No experiment removes one head and measures what that costs. None counts how many heads do anything describable. None connects a picture in the appendix to a point of BLEU.

The figures and the ablation are two separate kinds of statement about [[multi-head-attention]] — one about what a head appears to do, one about what head count is worth. The paper never joins them.

The other knobs turned the same one-at-a-time way are in [[transformer-ablations]].

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

n-per-position-parts--one-matrix-three-j.title: One vocabulary, or nothing to share
n-per-position-parts--one-matrix-three-j.intro:
Section 5.1 reports one number — a vocabulary of about 37000 tokens — and no method at all.

The method sits in the cited [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] paper. Three things about it matter here. It is a counting loop, not a trained model. It has exactly one hyperparameter. And that one hyperparameter sets a trade-off which quietly fixes the sequence length $n$ — the same $n$ the Transformer's own cost argument leans on.

This level walks the procedure first. Then it checks what the English-French vocabulary actually is.

chapters.title: The merge loop, in full
chapters.body:
[[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] has a learning step, but nothing in it is learned by gradient descent. [[bpe-merge-algorithm|That learning step]] is a counting loop run over training text. What it produces is an ordered list.

Start with the loop itself.

Write every word as a sequence of characters, with a special end-of-word symbol appended. The marker is there so that word boundaries survive decoding. Initialise the symbol vocabulary to the character set.

Then repeat the following $k$ times. Count how often each adjacent symbol pair occurs across the corpus. Take the pair with the highest count,

$$(A,B) = \arg\max_{(x,y)} \mathrm{count}(x,y)$$

and rewrite every occurrence of the bigram $A\,B$ as one new symbol $AB$. One merge, one new symbol, no exceptions.

Two implementation facts do a lot of work. The first is about boundaries. Pairs never cross word boundaries, so the loop never has to scan the corpus at all. It runs over a word-frequency dictionary instead, weighting each word's pair counts by that word's corpus frequency.

The second is about size. The whole thing fits in a short Python listing in the cited paper. `get_stats` counts weighted pairs over a dictionary of space-separated symbols. `merge_vocab` rewrites the winning pair with a whitespace-boundary regex. The outer loop runs `num_merges` times, recording each chosen pair in order.

The toy run trains on {low, lowest, newer, wider}. It learns, in order: `r·` (r plus end-of-word), then `l o → lo`, then `lo w → low`, then `e r· → er·`.

The ordering is the point. Frequent character n-grams become symbols first. Run the loop long enough and frequent whole words collapse to single symbols, while rare ones stay in pieces.

That ordered list is the entire model. No probabilities, no likelihood, no learned parameters.

[[joint-bpe-shared-vocabulary|Joint BPE]] changes exactly one thing: which pile of text the counts are taken over. The loop itself is identical. That is why the two variants cost the same to run and differ only in what comes out.

chapters.title: Replaying the merges on a word you have not seen
chapters.body:
Learning the merges and applying them are separate steps. The second step is what makes a fixed vocabulary behave like an open one.

[[bpe-segmentation-at-test-time|To segment any word]], split it into characters and append the end-of-word marker. Then replay the learned merges, in the order they were learned. Every symbol that comes out is by construction in the fixed symbol set — a merge can only ever produce a symbol the loop already created.

The toy example shows the effect. The word `lower` never appears in training. The merges learned from {low, lowest, newer, wider} still turn it into `low er·`. The cited paper reports zero unknown tokens on its test set under this scheme.

The guarantee is not quite airtight, and the cited paper says where it leaks. There are two holes.

First, a character not seen during training has no symbol to start from. There is nothing there to begin merging.

Second, a symbol can exist in the list and yet never survive as a standalone piece, because every training occurrence of it got merged into something larger. Put another way: it is in the vocabulary, but the model has never had to embed it alone.

The authors report observing neither at test time. They also note that the first could be handled by recursively reversing specific merges.

For [[wmt-2014-en-de|the English-German model]], this is the property that makes the whole scheme viable. [[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing|The single tied matrix]] has a fixed number of rows, and that number is decided before training starts.

Without test-time replay you would need an UNK row and a back-off story for rare names. With it, the row count is genuinely all the vocabulary the model ever needs.

Decoding runs the same machinery backwards. Concatenate the pieces, then cut at the end-of-word markers.

chapters.title: Where a number like 37000 comes from
chapters.body:
[[bpe-vocabulary-size|The size identity]] is exact. Each merge adds one symbol and removes none, so after $k$ merges

$$|V| = |V_{\text{chars}}| + k$$

where $V_{\text{chars}}$ is the character set of the training data.

Choosing $k$ therefore chooses the vocabulary size directly. And $k$ is the only knob the method has. No shortlist, no frequency cutoff, no separate segmentation model with its own parameters to fit. That is the cited paper's stated selling point over the alternatives it compares against.

Its own experiments set $k = 59{,}500$ for per-language [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] and $k = 89{,}500$ for [[joint-bpe-shared-vocabulary|joint BPE]]. Those are the numbers behind the roughly 80K-of-94K overlap figure.

The gap between the two settings is far from nothing. A joint run needs more merges than either language alone would, because the same budget is being spread over two languages' text.

One wrinkle stops the identity from being invertible in practice. The cited paper drops infrequent subword symbols that come out of corpus noise, mostly stray foreign-alphabet characters. So the vocabulary the network actually gets ends up slightly below $|V_{\text{chars}}| + k$.

"About 37000 tokens" therefore cannot be read backwards to a specific merge count. And [[wmt-2014-en-de|Section 5.1]] never states one.

What the figure does fix, exactly, is model shape. 37000 rows is the height of the tied matrix in [[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing|the three-way sharing]], and the same 37000 is the width of the output softmax.

Work the size out. Each row is [[d-model|$d_{model} = 512$]] wide, so the matrix holds around $37000 \times 512 \approx 19$M parameters. The base model has 65M parameters in total, so that one matrix is a sizeable fraction of it.

The tokenizer setting is a model-size decision.

chapters.title: The knob is really sequence length
chapters.body:
The merge count is presented in the cited paper as a position on a curve, not as a free choice. [[vocabulary-vs-sequence-length-tradeoff|The trade-off]] has two sides, pulling opposite ways.

On one side, a neural model wants a small vocabulary. Small is cheaper in time and in space, and it avoids back-off dictionaries.

On the other side, the same model wants compact text. Longer token sequences slow training and decoding, and they stretch the distance information has to travel. The cited paper notes that encoder-decoder time complexity is at least linear in sequence length.

The endpoints of the curve are measured. Take a 100M-token German corpus. Full character segmentation gives a vocabulary of about 3,000 types, and it inflates the corpus to 550M tokens. Around 60K merged types gives 112M tokens instead — roughly 12% longer than word-level tokenization — while still leaving zero unknowns.

Same text, five-fold difference in $n$, decided by one integer.

That integer lands in the middle of Section 4. [[table-1]] puts a self-attention layer at $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ per layer against a recurrent layer's $O(n \cdot d^2)$. Set the two against each other and the condition falls out: on [[complexity-per-layer|per-layer cost]], self-attention wins only when $n < d$.

The paper's defence of that condition is a pointer, not a measurement. It says $n < d$ is most often the case for the sentence representations state-of-the-art translation models use, "such as word-piece and byte-pair representations", and cites the two tokenizer papers.

So the cost argument rests on a tokenizer setting. At $d = 512$, a 25-word sentence has to come out as tens of tokens, not hundreds. [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] at tens of thousands of merges delivers that; character segmentation would not.

The paper never sweeps the merge count. It also never says how long its tokenized sentences actually are.

chapters.title: The French vocabulary, and what its own paper does
chapters.body:
[[wmt-2014-en-fr|The English-French run]] uses a 32000-token [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece vocabulary]]. That is a different algorithm, not a rebranded one.

Start with what it optimises. [[wordpiece-model|The cited scheme]] selects a fixed set of $D$ sub-word strings by a greedy search that maximises the language-model likelihood of the training data under the evolving vocabulary. Roughly: the $D$ pieces that segment the corpus into the fewest total tokens. Frequency of adjacent pairs is not the criterion.

The seed differs too. It is the basic character set, capped at a manageable size — around 500 for Western languages, more for Asian ones. The remaining rare characters are mapped to a single unknown-character symbol. So unlike [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]], this scheme has one escape hatch at the character level rather than none.

Word boundaries are recovered differently as well. The marker is prepended at the start of each word only, not attached at both ends. `Jet makers feud over seat width` becomes `_J et _makers _fe ud _over _seat _width`.

On size, the cited system reports 8k to 32k pieces as a good trade between accuracy and decoding speed. 32000 sits at the top of that band.

That is the algorithm. Now the loose end the parent flagged, which is whether this vocabulary is shared across source and target.

The cited system states that for translation it trains a single shared vocabulary over both source and target text, so an identical string segments identically on both sides. That is the same property [[joint-bpe-shared-vocabulary|joint BPE]] buys, reached by a different route.

Following the scheme as its own paper describes it therefore yields a shared vocabulary by default. [[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing|Section 3.4]] states the sharing with no exception, and this is consistent with it.

Neither paper confirms it for this model. That is where the evidence stops.

n-the-argument-in-three-numbers--where-t.title: What the three columns never price
n-the-argument-in-three-numbers--where-t.intro:
The parent node listed what the table leaves out. It named the omissions without pricing them.

This level does the arithmetic on each one. Three questions, in order: what the dropped constants actually weigh, how much of a real layer's work sits in the row that does not exist, and where in the paper each unpriced cost eventually gets settled.

chapters.title: Doing the constants by hand
chapters.body:
Big-O keeps the shape of a cost and throws away the multiplier in front of it. Two layers that both cost $O(n \cdot d^2)$ can differ by a factor of several, and the notation will not say so.

So put the constants back, one row at a time.

Start with the recurrent row: $O(n \cdot d^2)$. Where does that shape come from? At each of the $n$ steps, the layer multiplies a $d$-dimensional hidden state by a $d \times d$ matrix. That is $d^2$ multiply-adds per step, over $n$ steps, so $n \cdot d^2$ for the layer.

A plain [[recurrent-neural-network|RNN]] cell does roughly that and not much more. An [[lstm]] does considerably more. It computes four gated pre-activations at every step, and each of the four has its own input matrix and its own recurrent matrix.

The shape does not change. Still $n$ steps, still $d \times d$ multiplies. The constant in front is several times larger. A [[gated-recurrent-unit|GRU]] has fewer gates than an LSTM and more machinery than a plain cell, so it sits somewhere between the two.

Three cells, three different constants. All three land in the same cell of [[table-1]].

Now the self-attention row, $O(n^2 \cdot d)$. This one hides something more interesting than a constant. It hides a term of a different shape.

[[multi-head-attention]] does not attend directly to the vectors coming into the sub-layer. It projects them first. [[attention-projection-matrices|$W^Q$, $W^K$ and $W^V$]] turn each position's vector into a query, a key, and a value, and after the heads are concatenated, $W^O$ mixes the result back to model width.

Count those projections. Across all [[num-heads-h|eight heads]] together, the queries account for one full $512 \times 512$ map, the keys another, the values a third, and $W^O$ a fourth. A $512 \times 512$ map is 262144 multiply-adds, and four of them come to about 1.05M — per position.

Multiply by $n$ positions and that is an $n \cdot d^2$ term. It is sitting inside a row labelled $n^2 \cdot d$.

The paper's own justification for not writing that term down is a claim about the constant. Because [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h$]] — that is 512 split across 8 heads, so 64 dimensions each — [[eq-multihead|the total cost of multi-head attention]] is *similar* to single-head attention at full dimensionality.

Similar, not equal.

One more constant, and it is the plainest of the three. Every row of the table prices a single layer.

The [[encoder-stack]] is [[n-layers|six]] layers. The [[decoder-stack]] is six more. And a decoder layer is not the same object as an encoder layer: it carries two attention [[sub-layer|sub-layers]] rather than one.

Nothing in the table multiplies by any of that. The [[complexity-per-layer|per-layer]] framing is stated honestly, right in the column heading, so the table is not concealing it. It is simply not the number you pay.

chapters.title: The sub-layer with no row
chapters.body:
Constants are one thing. The larger gap is a whole sub-layer with no row at all.

Every encoder layer and every decoder layer contains a [[position-wise-feed-forward-network]]. The table has three rows for layer types and none for that. So count it the way the table counts everything else.

[[eq-ffn|The block]] is two matrix multiplies with a nonlinearity between them. It widens each position's vector from [[d-model|512]] to [[d-ff|2048]], applies a [[relu|ReLU]], and projects back down to 512.

So each position passes through a $512 \times 2048$ matrix going up and a $2048 \times 512$ matrix coming back. $512 \times 2048$ is a little over 1M multiply-adds, and there are two of them, so about 2.1M per position.

Write that in the table's own variables. Since $d_{ff} = 4 d_{model}$, each of the two multiplies costs $4 d^2$, giving $8 d^2$ per position and roughly $8 n d^2$ per layer.

Now the thing to compare it against: the part of the attention sub-layer the table does price. Every query is dotted against every key, which is $n^2$ dot products of length $d$. Then every output is a weighted sum over $n$ values, which is another $n^2$ accumulations of width $d$. About $2 n^2 d$ in total.

Set the two expressions equal. $8 n d^2 = 2 n^2 d$ gives $n = 4d$, and with $d$ at 512 that crossover sits near 2048 tokens.

Below 2048, the feed-forward sub-layer is doing more arithmetic than the attention sub-layer it follows. Only above 2048 does attention take over.

The paper's sequences are nothing like 2048 tokens long. Sentence pairs are grouped into batches holding about 25000 tokens in total, and an individual sentence is far shorter than that.

Put the two facts side by side. On the paper's own workload, most of the multiply-adds in a layer live in a row that does not appear.

The paper does acknowledge the pairing once. Not in the table — in the prose of Section 4, while arguing about [[convolutional-sequence-models|convolutions]].

It notes there that [[separable-convolutions|a separable convolution]] at kernel width $k = n$ costs $O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$, and calls that equal to "the combination of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed-forward layer, the approach we take in our model."

Notice what that sentence does. It adds the two sub-layers together, because the separable convolution has a per-position term of its own and the comparison would otherwise be unfair.

The rows of [[table-1]] never do that addition.

chapters.title: Holding the score matrix
chapters.body:
The first column counts the $n \times n$ scores as arithmetic. It prices the work of producing them and then moves on.

But the scores are not only work. They are numbers, and numbers have to sit somewhere.

Count what is resident. Each [[attention-head|head]] scores every position against every other position, so each head produces its own $n \times n$ matrix.

Eight heads, so one [[encoder-self-attention|encoder self-attention]] sub-layer holds $8 n^2$ floats of raw scores. The [[softmax]] does not shrink that — the normalized weights have exactly the same shape, so there is a second $8 n^2$ after it.

Then multiply out. Six encoder layers. Six decoder layers with two attention sub-layers each. And every example in the batch carries its own copy of all of it.

None of it can be released early either. The [[eq-attention|weighted sum]] needs its weights again on the backward pass in order to produce gradients, so the whole set stays alive from the forward pass until the gradient comes back through.

Against that, a recurrent layer stores $n \cdot d$ activations. Quadratic in $n$ on one side, linear in $n$ on the other — and this at exactly the sequence lengths where the arithmetic columns say self-attention is the cheaper of the two.

The paper is not unaware of memory. The phrase "space-efficient" does appear, once, in the [[dot-product-attention|dot-product]] versus [[additive-attention|additive]] comparison. But there it is a remark about how the operation is implemented, not about how much a layer keeps resident.

Section 4's only response to anything quadratic is [[restricted-self-attention]]: let each position attend only within a neighbourhood of size $r$ around it. It is offered as a fix for computation on very long sequences, and the cost of the fix is booked in the [[maximum-path-length|path-length]] column, which rises to $O(n/r)$.

What it would do to stored activations goes unmentioned. So does whether the authors ran it at all; they say only that they plan to investigate it in future work.

A fourth column, for what a layer holds, would put the sequence-length ceiling a practitioner actually hits on the face of [[table-1]].

There are three.

chapters.title: The column for the clock
chapters.body:
All three columns are asymptotic, and that makes them blind to one particular kind of question. If two designs scale the same way, the columns have nothing to say about which one to pick.

The paper faces exactly that choice once. It breaks the tie, elsewhere in the text, on grounds the table cannot express.

The choice is between [[additive-attention]] and [[dot-product-attention]], in Section 3.2.1. The paper says the two are "similar in theoretical complexity." That is the [[complexity-per-layer|first column]] declining to decide.

It picks the dot product anyway, because the dot product "is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code."

Read what that argument is about. Not how many operations there are — on that count the two are similar, by the paper's own statement. It is about what the hardware does with the operations it is handed. Additive attention scores a query-key pair with a small feed-forward layer, and that hidden layer does not collapse into a single dense matmul. The dot product does.

The same section carries a second decision that no column can price at all.

Dot products taken over $d_k$ dimensions grow in magnitude as $d_k$ grows. Large scores push the [[softmax]] into a region where its gradients are very small. So [[scaled-dot-product-attention]] divides every score by [[sqrt-dk-scaling|$\sqrt{d_k}$]] before the softmax.

That is one scalar multiply. It changes no exponent and moves no constant worth naming. The paper suspects that training turns on it — suspects, which is the paper's own strength of claim, not demonstrates.

In the three columns, that division ranks exactly level with doing nothing.

Real clock numbers do exist in the paper. They arrive in Sections 5 and 6, well after Section 4 has finished arguing.

The base model runs 100,000 steps in about twelve hours on [[training-hardware-and-schedule|eight P100s]]. Twelve hours is 43200 seconds, so that works out to roughly 0.4 seconds a step. And [[table-2]]'s cost axis is not measured throughput at all — it is a [[training-flops-estimate|FLOPs estimate]], built from training time, the number of GPUs, and an assumed sustained throughput per GPU.

Those numbers describe one implementation, in [[tensor2tensor]], on one machine. They belong to a different argument than the one Section 4 is making.

chapters.title: What one hop costs in resolution
chapters.body:
The omissions so far have all been resources: constants, arithmetic, memory. The last one is not a resource. It is quality.

A path of length 1 means one position reaches another in a single step. That is what the third column records, and it is true.

Now look at what the single step consists of. It is a weighted average over every position at once. Every position contributes its value; the weights decide how much.

And [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost|averaging blurs]]. Section 3.2.2 says so flatly: with a single attention head, averaging inhibits attending to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

So the one-hop entry in [[table-1]] prices the reach. It does not price the blur.

[[multi-head-attention]] is the stated repair, and its shape is one the [[layer-comparison-desiderata|three criteria]] could never have motivated.

The shape is this: instead of one attention function at the full width of 512, run eight in parallel at width 64 each. The widths are picked so the total comes back to 512, which keeps total computation roughly fixed.

Which means the first column reads the same either way. One head or eight, the complexity entry does not move. Whatever design pressure produced this came from somewhere the columns do not look.

What the repair buys does get measured — later, and by a different instrument.

In [[table-3]], rows (A) vary the head count with total computation held constant. [[attention-heads-ablation|Single-head attention comes out 0.9 BLEU worse]] than the best setting. Quality also drops off at the other end, with too many heads.

Rows (B) vary the key dimension instead. [[key-size-ablation|Shrinking $d_k$ hurts]], and the paper reads that as a hint — a hint, not a finding — that a dot product may be too simple a [[compatibility-function]].

Two caveats attach to both. Each is a single run on a development set. And each arrives two sections after the decision it bears on.

So each unpriced cost is settled somewhere else in the paper, or not at all.

Head count is settled by ablation. Speed is settled by an appeal to what the implementation does on the hardware, together with [[table-2]]'s estimated cost axis. Memory is settled by nothing published here.

[[etheme-case-against-recurrence]] and [[theme-why-self-attention]] put the three columns back in their place in the argument.

n-training-the-thing--three-regularizers.title: What the citation actually says
n-training-the-thing--three-regularizers.intro:
The summary above gave the formula and the motive. This level opens the cited section itself.

Four things are in it. Where the mixture comes from, before it is a formula at all. What the two knobs would do if anyone turned them. What the split loss does to the numbers a training run prints. And how much evidence stood behind $\epsilon = 0.1$ at the moment it was carried across from vision.

chapters.title: Where the mixture comes from
chapters.body:
The cited section does not open with the mixture. It opens with a procedure. The mixture is what you get by averaging over that procedure.

Here is the procedure. Draw the training label by setting it to the reference token $y$. Then, with probability $\epsilon$, throw that draw away and replace it with a token drawn from $u$ instead. The label you train on depends on how that coin lands. [[label-smoothing-regularization|LSR]] is what you train against when you skip the flip and use its expected target directly. The cited paper's own framing of the section is estimating the marginalized effect of label dropout.

The notation it sets up is worth carrying, because the later steps lean on it. $z_k$ are the logits. $p(k) = \exp(z_k)/\sum_i \exp(z_i)$ is the [[softmax]] over $K$ classes. And $q(k|x)$ is the ground-truth distribution, required only to be normalized.

The loss is then written $\ell = -\sum_k q(k)\log p(k)$, for an arbitrary target. The one-hot case arrives a paragraph later, as a specialization rather than as the premise. That order is what pays off two steps on: because the loss was never tied to a one-hot target in the first place, the decomposition is available for free.

That is the setup as the vision paper leaves it. Moving it to translation changes the unit.

A class here is an entry in the output vocabulary. And the classifier runs at every decoder position, rather than once per image. The [[masked-decoder-self-attention|decoder]] emits one token per position under [[auto-regressive-generation|the auto-regressive constraint]], and batches are assembled to roughly 25000 target tokens by [[length-based-batching|approximate sequence length]].

So the smoothed target is applied about 25000 times per step. What [[label-smoothing|Section 5.4]] states as a single value of 0.1 is, at each of those positions, a tenth of the target mass reassigned away from the reference token. Every one of those positions is scored by [[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing|the projection shared with the embedding tables]].

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

chapters.title: Two knobs, and the one nobody turned
chapters.body:
The cited work proposes using the prior distribution over classes as $u$. It then reports experiments that use uniform $u$ anyway.

So the gap between the proposal and the setting is already there in the source, before anything is carried anywhere. This paper inherits the setting and drops the proposal. [[smoothing-parameter-epsilon|Both knobs]] survive the transfer, but only one of them gets a number.

The choice matters more here than it did there. A thousand photo classes are roughly balanced. A 37000-symbol vocabulary built by [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] is not — frequent subwords and rare ones differ by orders of magnitude in how often they occur in the corpus.

Under uniform $u$, none of that registers. The floor is $2.7 \times 10^{-6}$ for a comma. It is the same $2.7 \times 10^{-6}$ for a piece that appears a few dozen times across 4.5M sentence pairs. A corpus-prior $u$ would put the floor where the mass actually is. Neither paper reports trying it.

The two training runs make the asymmetry visible. [[wmt-2014-en-de|English-German]] uses about 37000 shared BPE tokens. [[wmt-2014-en-fr|English-French]] uses a 32000-entry [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] vocabulary.

$\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1$ is stated once and covers both. So the mass taken off the reference token is 0.1 in each run. But that mass is spread across a different number of symbols in each, and the per-wrong-token floor is correspondingly not the same: $2.7 \times 10^{-6}$ against $3.1 \times 10^{-6}$.

Put another way: $\epsilon$ is the setting. The floor is downstream of a vocabulary decision made for unrelated reasons.

As for the value, 0.1 arrives from the vision paper unchanged. There is no sweep. $\epsilon_{ls}$ is not a row in [[table-3]], which varies head count, $d_k$, model size, [[dropout]] rate and [[positional-encoding]], and stops there. [[transformer-training-recipe|The recipe]] reports smoothing as settled rather than as chosen.

chapters.title: What the split loss does to the numbers
chapters.body:
The identity itself was in the summary above. Two things follow from it that the identity does not show on its face. Take them in order.

First, the weight. Factor $(1-\epsilon)$ out of the front, and what is left attached to the second loss is its weight relative to the first: $\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)$. At $\epsilon = 0.1$ that is $0.1/0.9$ — exactly one ninth.

[[lsr-as-two-cross-entropy-losses|The pair]] is lopsided by construction. The pull toward $u$ is a standing tax on the ordinary objective, not a co-equal term.

Second, the constant. Cross entropy against $u$ decomposes as $H(u,p) = D_{KL}(u\|p) + H(u)$, and the second piece has no model in it. For uniform $u$ over 37000 symbols, $H(u) = \log 37000 \approx 10.5$ nats. That number is added to every example's loss and never moves. Only the divergence part carries a gradient.

The consequence is for anyone reading the printed loss. A smoothed run's reported loss is displaced from an unsmoothed one by a fixed offset, plus a term measuring distance from uniform. The two curves are not on a common scale.

The quantity being minimized is no longer the log-likelihood that [[perplexity]] exponentiates.

Both the offset and the floor also move when the vocabulary moves. [[bpe-vocabulary-size|The merge count sets $K$]], and $K$ is picked against [[vocabulary-vs-sequence-length-tradeoff|tokenized sequence length]] — a trade-off that has nothing to do with smoothing.

One alternative in the cited text went untaken. When $u$ is uniform, $H(u,p)$ measures how far $p$ sits from uniform. So does negative entropy $-H(p)$, though the cited paper is careful to say not equivalently. Its own sentence about the swap is that they have not experimented with this approach.

So the entropy-penalty form of this [[regularization|regularizer]] is untested in the work being cited. It is untested here as well.

chapters.title: The argument, and what was behind it
chapters.body:
The cited case against one-hot targets has two limbs, and only one of them is about confidence.

The first limb: a model that learns to assign full probability to the training label at every example is not guaranteed to generalize.

The second limb is about the route to that target rather than the target itself. Assigning full probability requires the correct logit to run far ahead of all the others. And the per-logit gradient of cross entropy is bounded:

$$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_k} = p(k) - q(k) \in [-1, 1]$$

So a widening gap has to be bought one bounded step at a time, which the source says reduces the model's ability to adapt. [[overconfidence-and-bounded-logit-gradient|The whole argument]] is hedged where it is made — may result in over-fitting, intuitively.

Substituting $q'$ makes the fix legible in the same expression, one token at a time.

At the reference token the gradient becomes $p(y) - (1 - \epsilon + \epsilon/K)$. That reaches zero at $p(y) \approx 0.9$, instead of never. At any other token it is $p(k) - \epsilon/K$, which turns positive as soon as $p(k)$ falls below $2.7 \times 10^{-6}$, so the model is pushed back up toward the floor.

The source's own reason this works: every $q'(k)$ has a positive lower bound, unlike $\delta_{k,y}$, so a runaway top logit is charged a large cross entropy.

That upward push lands on shared weights. The projection is [[weight-tying|tied]] to both embedding tables — [[three-way-weight-tying|three roles, one matrix]]. So a gradient on 37000 output rows is a gradient on 37000 [[token-embeddings|embedding rows]].

[[tied-embedding-update-dynamics|The tying argument]] is that the output matrix already gets an update on every row every step. On that view, smoothing changes what the tail updates say rather than adding them. Neither paper discusses the interaction.

The evidence carried over is thin. In the source, smoothing is one row of a cumulative table on ILSVRC 2012: top-1 error 23.1% to 22.8%, top-5 6.3% to 6.1%. That is roughly the 0.2% absolute the text claims.

But the row is cumulative, with every earlier change still stacked in. It is not the one-at-a-time design of [[transformer-ablations|the ablations here]].

That is the basis on which $\epsilon = 0.1$ arrives at a 37000-way conditional model for [[machine-translation]].

n-what-the-numbers-show--one-knob-at-a-t.title: Where the BLEU is bought
n-what-the-numbers-show--one-knob-at-a-t.intro:
The parent level gave you the row values. This level takes them apart.

Four questions run through it. What does each knob actually change inside the model. Where do the parameters land when a number goes up. Which rows move two things at once, so that the effect you are reading is not the effect the row is labelled with. And what are the two result columns each measuring, in the places where they disagree.

chapters.title: Depth, and the column that stays monotone
chapters.body:
Start with depth. Four rows in [[table-3]] vary it, counting the base configuration as one of them. Read them together and the table's two result columns do not behave the same way.

[[perplexity|Perplexity]] is monotone in [[n-layers|$N$]]. At 2 layers it is 6.11. At 4 layers it is 5.19. At 6 — the base — it is 4.92. At 8 it is 4.88. Every layer added helps, and every layer added helps less than the one before it.

[[bleu|BLEU]] does not do that. Over the same four depths it runs 23.7, 25.3, 25.8, 25.5. It peaks at the base depth and then comes back down.

So the reading is not that depth stops paying. On the metric the model is actually trained against, it never stops paying. What stops is the second column following the first past $N = 6$.

That is the shape of the result. Now what it costs.

The yield per parameter collapses fast. Going from 2 layers to 4 costs 14M parameters and returns 1.6 BLEU. Going from 4 to 8 costs 30M parameters and returns 0.2.

One detail sits behind those parameter counts. $N$ counts layers in both stacks at once — the [[encoder-stack|encoder]] and the [[decoder-stack|decoder]] grow together, layer for layer. That is why the 8-layer row lands at 80M parameters rather than somewhere nearer 70M.

There is also one thing this row group holds fixed that is easy to walk past. Every row here trains for 100K steps at [[residual-dropout|$P_{drop} = 0.1$]], which is the base setting. Meanwhile the parameter counts across all of [[size-and-dropout-ablation|group (C)]] range from 36M up to 168M.

Set that against the last row of the table. The [[base-vs-big-transformer|big model]] runs $P_{drop} = 0.3$ and [[training-hardware-and-schedule|300K steps]]. So the large (C) rows are regularized and trained like a 65M model, whatever their actual size.

The paper does not raise this. And the table gives no way to tell how much of the flattening at $N = 8$ is depth running out and how much is a fixed schedule.

chapters.title: Width moves two things at once
chapters.body:
The [[d-model|$d_{model}$]] rows look like a width sweep. They are not a clean one, and the table's own configuration columns are what give it away.

Look at what else changes down those rows. At $d_{model} = 256$ the row also lists [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = 32$]]. At $d_{model} = 1024$ it lists 128. Neither of those is a separate decision the authors made.

Both are forced by the arithmetic. [[num-heads-h|$h$]] is held at 8 across the group, and the per-head width is $d_{model}/h$. So at 256, each head gets $256/8 = 32$ dimensions. At 1024, each head gets $1024/8 = 128$. Change the model width and you have changed every head's width with it.

That matters because another row group already measured the key dimension on its own. In [[key-size-ablation|rows (B)]], cutting $d_k$ to 32 while leaving $d_{model}$ at 512 costs 0.4 BLEU.

The 256 row does two things at once. It cuts $d_k$ to 32 *and* it halves the model. It loses 1.3 BLEU.

The two effects are not separable from the table. (B) held the model width fixed, so its 0.4 is not a quantity you can subtract from the 1.3 to leave a clean width penalty behind. What the comparison does show is that part of what reads as a width penalty is the narrower keys inside [[multi-head-attention|each head]].

The paper's own scale-up avoids the tangle. The big model takes $d_{model}$ to 1024 and raises $h$ to 16 at the same time. Since $1024/16 = 64$, $d_k = d_v = 64$ is unchanged from the base. Row (C) never does that.

That is the confound. Now the cost, which is where width turns out to be the expensive direction structurally.

$d_{model}$ is fixed everywhere in the model by [[residual-connection|the residual connections]] — every sub-layer's output has to be addable to that sub-layer's input, so they all carry the same width. Raising it therefore does not touch one place. It touches all of them.

The [[attention-projection-matrices|four projection matrices]] in all 18 attention blocks get wider, and they get wider quadratically, because both their input dimension and their output dimension scale with $d_{model}$. [[token-embeddings|The embedding table]], [[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing|shared three ways]], grows only linearly.

The quadratic part is what dominates the bill. Doubling $d_{model}$ takes the model from 65M parameters to 168M, for 0.2 BLEU.

chapters.title: The feed-forward layer as the cheap axis
chapters.body:
[[d-ff|$d_{ff}$]] is the one knob in group (C) that touches nothing else in the model.

It appears in exactly one place: between the two matrices of [[eq-ffn|Equation (2)]], $\max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2$. $W_1$ maps $d_{model}$ up to $d_{ff}$, and $W_2$ maps it back down. So widening $d_{ff}$ widens those two matrices and leaves every other dimension in the model exactly where it was. No head width changes. No residual width changes.

It is also linear in parameters rather than quadratic, and the table's own counts show that exactly. Walk the arithmetic.

Each of the 12 [[position-wise-feed-forward-network|feed-forward sub-layers]] — one per layer, six layers in each stack — holds $2 \cdot d_{model} \cdot d_{ff}$ weights. At the base setting that is $2 \cdot 512 \cdot 2048$, about 2.1M per sub-layer. Across all 12, about 25M. That is roughly 40% of the base model's 65M.

Now check the two rows against that number. Halving $d_{ff}$ to 1024 should remove about half of the 25M, so about 12.6M; the table reports 53M, down from 65M. Doubling $d_{ff}$ to 4096 should add another 25M; the table reports 90M. Both land where the arithmetic puts them.

So set the best feed-forward row against the widest model row. It is 26.2 BLEU at 90M parameters against 26.0 BLEU at 168M. On the other column it is 4.75 [[perplexity|PPL]] against 4.66.

The two columns split here. Perplexity still prefers the wide model. BLEU prefers the wide feed-forward layer, at 78M fewer parameters.

Be precise about what the 4096 row actually is. It is a model whose inner feed-forward layer is eight times $d_{model}$, rather than the four times that Section 3.3 specifies.

That ratio of four is stated in the architecture section as a fact about the base configuration. It is never presented as a choice with a reason behind it.

[[transformer-ablations|The ablation]] tests it once. It gets the best base-depth row in the table. Section 6.2 then folds that result into a single sentence about bigger models being better. The [[relu|ReLU]] block sitting between the two matrices goes uncommented.

chapters.title: One dropout number, three places
chapters.body:
[[dropout|Dropout]] is a single column in the table, but it is not a single application.

Section 5.4 puts [[residual-dropout|residual dropout]] on the output of every [[sub-layer|sub-layer]] — applied before that output is added back to the sub-layer's input and passed through [[layer-normalization|layer normalization]]. It applies dropout separately to the sums of the embeddings and [[positional-encoding|positional encodings]], in both stacks.

One rate, $P_{drop}$, sets all of those. So the 0.0 row is not removing dropout from one place. It removes it everywhere at once.

The penalty for getting the rate wrong is asymmetric.

Going from 0.0 up to the base 0.1 is worth 1.2 BLEU and 0.85 perplexity. Going from 0.1 up to 0.2 costs 0.3 BLEU and 0.03 perplexity.

So the optimum is interior — the base sits at neither end of the range tested — but the curve is much steeper on the low side. That is the shape you would expect if the base model sits closer to overfitting than to underfitting on 4.5M sentence pairs.

One calibration for how large that 1.2 BLEU is. The undropped model scores 24.6 BLEU. The model with $d_{model}$ halved scores 24.5, at 37M fewer parameters. Put another way: turning off [[regularization|the regularizer]] costs about what deleting more than half the model costs.

Note also which way the two result columns move across this row group. They move together. A worse dropout setting means worse perplexity and worse BLEU, in both directions away from the base. That is what makes the next pair of rows odd rather than routine.

One more gap in the same section. Section 5.4 announces three types of regularization and then describes two. [[attention-dropout|Dropout inside attention]] surfaces only as a separately tuned rate in the parsing experiments, and [[table-3]] has no column for it.

chapters.title: Why the two result columns split
chapters.body:
On the smoothing axis the two columns come apart.

Perplexity is monotone in $\epsilon_{ls}$, and it is monotone the wrong way: 4.67 at 0.0, 4.92 at the base 0.1, 5.47 at 0.2. More smoothing, worse perplexity, at every step.

BLEU over the same three rows goes 25.3, 25.8, 25.7. Up sharply, then essentially flat. Across the full range, perplexity degrades by 0.8 while BLEU does not fall at all.

The mechanism is in what [[label-smoothing|smoothing]] does to the training target.

[[label-smoothing-regularization|The cited construction]] replaces the one-hot target with a mixture. [[smoothing-parameter-epsilon|$1 - \epsilon$ goes on the correct token]], and $\epsilon$ is spread over the rest — here uniformly, across a 37000-entry [[byte-pair-encoding|word-piece vocabulary]].

Cross entropy against that target [[lsr-as-two-cross-entropy-losses|splits into two terms]]. One is the ordinary one-hot loss. The other is a pull toward the flat prior.

The consequence is that training never asks for probability 1 on the reference token. So the model never drives the correct logit far above the others. That is exactly [[overconfidence-and-bounded-logit-gradient|the overconfidence the cited paper is trying to prevent]].

Which is why the columns disagree. Perplexity is measuring the mass the model was trained to hold back. It reads the [[softmax]] probability on the true [[word-piece-encoding|word piece]], token by token, and a deliberately flattened distribution scores worse on that reading by construction.

BLEU reads something else. It reads what [[beam-search]] emits. And beam search depends on which hypothesis outranks which, not on how peaked the distribution is at any single step.

The practical consequence sits in the table without being drawn out. The $\epsilon_{ls} = 0.0$ row has the lowest perplexity of any row that keeps the base's 65M parameters. It also gives up half a BLEU. Selecting a translation model on dev perplexity would pick it.
